major.suprascapular.name: Suprascapular nerve
major.suprascapular.root_values: Arises from the superior trunk of the brachial plexus; root values C5 and C6.
major.suprascapular.course: Passes through the suprascapular notch, inferior to the superior transverse scapular ligament, to reach the posterior scapular region.
major.suprascapular.sensory_distribution: None — the nerve has no cutaneous branches.
verify: clinical_testing: no bedside test or lesion pattern specific to the suprascapular nerve is stated in the consulted sources; not entered - verify
major.suprascapular.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.long-thoracic.name: Long thoracic nerve
major.long-thoracic.root_values: Arises from the roots of the brachial plexus; root values C5, C6 and C7 (ventral primary rami).
major.long-thoracic.course: Descends on the superficial surface of the serratus anterior muscle.
major.long-thoracic.sensory_distribution: None — the nerve has no cutaneous branches.
major.long-thoracic.clinical_testing: Lesion of the nerve causes winging of the scapula (scapular winging), through paralysis of its muscle, the serratus anterior.
major.long-thoracic.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.musculocutaneous.name: Musculocutaneous nerve
major.musculocutaneous.root_values: Terminal branch of the lateral cord of the brachial plexus; root values C5, C6 and C7.
major.musculocutaneous.course: Arises in the axilla, pierces the coracobrachialis, then descends between the biceps brachii and brachialis muscles, and continues beyond the elbow as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
major.musculocutaneous.motor_distribution: Coracobrachialis, biceps brachii and brachialis — the muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm.
major.musculocutaneous.sensory_distribution: Continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, supplying the skin of the lateral side of the forearm.
major.musculocutaneous.clinical_testing: Injury to the nerve weakens flexion of the elbow and of the shoulder, and weakens supination of the forearm, with sensory loss over the lateral forearm.
major.musculocutaneous.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.axillary.name: Axillary nerve
major.axillary.root_values: Terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus; root values C5 and C6.
major.axillary.course: Arises in the axilla, exits the axilla through the quadrangular space, and winds around the surgical neck of the humerus to reach the deltoid.
major.axillary.sensory_distribution: Via its branch, the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm: the skin over the inferior part of the deltoid — the 'regimental badge' area.
major.axillary.clinical_testing: Most commonly injured by fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus or by shoulder dislocation: the deltoid is paralysed, so the arm cannot be abducted beyond the initial 15 degrees (the range supplied by supraspinatus), with sensory loss over the regimental badge area. Named bedside tests in the source include the deltoid extension lag sign and the external rotation lag sign.
major.axillary.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.radial.name: Radial nerve
major.radial.root_values: Terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus; root values C5–T1.
major.radial.course: Arises in the axilla, leaves via the triangular interval into the posterior compartment of the arm, descends in the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus, crosses anterior to the lateral epicondyle at the elbow, and divides into a deep branch — which passes through the supinator and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve — and a superficial sensory branch.
major.radial.motor_distribution: Triceps brachii, brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus, and — via the deep / posterior interosseous branch — the extensor muscles of the posterior compartment of the forearm.
major.radial.sensory_distribution: The posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm, the lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm and the posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm; and, via the superficial branch, the dorsal surface of the lateral three and a half digits.
major.radial.clinical_testing: Lesion in the axilla: paralysis of the triceps as well as of the wrist extensors, giving wrist drop. Lesion in the radial groove: wrist drop, but the triceps is weakened rather than paralysed (its branches arise proximal to the groove). Lesion of the deep branch alone: no wrist drop (extensor carpi radialis longus is spared) and no sensory loss.
major.radial.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.median.name: Median nerve
major.median.root_values: Formed in the axilla by the lateral and medial roots, from the lateral and medial cords of the brachial plexus; root values C6–T1, with C5 fibres present in some people.
major.median.course: Descends through the arm, first lateral and then medial to the brachial artery; passes through the cubital fossa, between the two heads of pronator teres, and deep to flexor digitorum superficialis in the forearm; enters the hand through the carpal tunnel and divides into the recurrent branch and the palmar digital branches.
major.median.motor_distribution: In the forearm: pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus and flexor digitorum superficialis; via the anterior interosseous branch: flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus. In the hand: the thenar muscles and the lateral two lumbricals.
major.median.sensory_distribution: The palmar cutaneous branch supplies the lateral part of the palm; the palmar digital branches supply the palmar surface of the lateral three and a half digits.
major.median.clinical_testing: Carpal tunnel syndrome is assessed with Tinel's sign and Phalen's manoeuvre; the palmar cutaneous branch is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome, because it does not pass through the carpal tunnel. A lesion at the elbow produces the 'hand of benediction' on attempted finger flexion, a supinated forearm and thenar wasting; a lesion at the wrist affects only the hand, the forearm muscles being spared.
major.median.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.ulnar.name: Ulnar nerve
major.ulnar.root_values: Continuation of the medial cord of the brachial plexus; root values C8 and T1.
major.ulnar.course: Arises in the axilla and descends the medial side of the arm; at mid-arm it penetrates the medial intermuscular septum into the posterior compartment, passes behind the elbow through the ulnar tunnel (between the medial epicondyle and the olecranon), pierces the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, and runs deep to that muscle in the forearm; at the wrist it passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum and enters the hand through the ulnar (Guyon's) canal, dividing into superficial and deep branches.
major.ulnar.motor_distribution: In the forearm: flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus. In the hand, via the deep branch: the hypothenar muscles, the medial two lumbricals, adductor pollicis and the palmar and dorsal interossei; palmaris brevis via the superficial branch. Together, all the intrinsic muscles of the hand except the thenar muscles and the lateral two lumbricals.
major.ulnar.sensory_distribution: The palmar cutaneous branch supplies the medial half of the palm; the dorsal cutaneous branch supplies the dorsal surface of the medial one and a half fingers and the associated dorsal hand; the superficial branch supplies the palmar surface of the medial one and a half fingers.
major.ulnar.clinical_testing: Froment's sign: the patient holds a piece of paper between thumb and index finger while the examiner pulls it away; if the adductor pollicis is paralysed, the thumb's interphalangeal joint flexes to hold the paper — a positive sign. Lesion at the elbow (for example medial epicondyle trauma or cubital tunnel compression): all ulnar muscles are affected, wrist flexion occurs with abduction, finger abduction and adduction are lost, Froment's sign is positive, all sensory branches are lost and the hypothenar eminence wastes. Lesion at the wrist: only the intrinsic hand muscles are affected, and the dorsal cutaneous branch is spared, so sensory loss is confined to the palmar medial one and a half fingers.
major.ulnar.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.medial-cutaneous-arm.name: Medial cutaneous nerve of arm
major.medial-cutaneous-arm.root_values: Branch of the medial cord of the brachial plexus (root values C8 and T1 via the cord).
major.medial-cutaneous-arm.course: Arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus; communicates with the intercostobrachial nerve.
major.medial-cutaneous-arm.sensory_distribution: Skin of the medial side of the arm.

major.medial-cutaneous-forearm.root_values: Branch of the medial cord of the brachial plexus (root values C8 and T1 via the cord).
major.medial-cutaneous-forearm.course: Arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus; travels with the basilic vein for part of its course.
major.medial-cutaneous-forearm.sensory_distribution: Skin of the medial side of the forearm.

major.femoral.name: Femoral nerve
major.femoral.root_values: The largest branch of the lumbar plexus, formed from the anterior rami of L2, L3 and L4.
major.femoral.course: Travels inferiorly through the substance of psoas major, passes under the inguinal ligament into the femoral triangle, lateral to the femoral vessels and outside the femoral sheath, and about 4 cm below the inguinal ligament divides into anterior and posterior divisions.
major.femoral.motor_distribution: Hip flexors: pectineus, iliacus and sartorius. Knee extensors: the quadriceps femoris (rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis and vastus intermedius).
major.femoral.sensory_distribution: The anterior cutaneous branches supply the anteromedial thigh; the saphenous nerve, its terminal branch, supplies the medial side of the leg and foot.
major.femoral.clinical_testing: In a lumbar plexopathy affecting the femoral nerve: weakness of hip flexion, impaired knee extension, and a reduced patellar reflex.
major.femoral.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.obturator.name: Obturator nerve
major.obturator.root_values: Formed from the anterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2, L3 and L4 (lumbar plexus).
major.obturator.course: Descends through the fibres of psoas major and emerges from its medial border, travels along the lateral pelvic wall to the obturator foramen, and enters the medial compartment of the thigh through the obturator canal, dividing into anterior and posterior divisions that pass in front of and behind adductor brevis.
major.obturator.motor_distribution: The muscles of the medial compartment of the thigh — adductor longus, adductor brevis, the adductor part of adductor magnus, gracilis and obturator externus — the hip adductors, excepting the hamstring part of adductor magnus.
major.obturator.sensory_distribution: Via its cutaneous branch: the skin of the middle part of the medial thigh.
major.obturator.clinical_testing: The nerve can be damaged during pelvic or abdominal surgery, causing numbness and paraesthesia on the medial side of the thigh, weakness of thigh adduction, and problems with posture and gait arising from the loss of adduction.
major.obturator.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.lateral-femoral-cutaneous.name: Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh
major.lateral-femoral-cutaneous.root_values: Branch of the lumbar plexus; root values L2 and L3.
major.lateral-femoral-cutaneous.course: Arises from the lumbar plexus and enters the thigh at the lateral aspect of the inguinal ligament.
major.lateral-femoral-cutaneous.motor_distribution: None — the nerve is purely sensory.
major.lateral-femoral-cutaneous.sensory_distribution: The skin of the anterior and lateral aspects of the thigh, down to the knee.
major.lateral-femoral-cutaneous.clinical_testing: In a lumbar plexopathy, involvement of this nerve produces sensory loss over the lateral thigh.
major.lateral-femoral-cutaneous.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.saphenous.name: Saphenous nerve
major.saphenous.root_values: Terminal branch of the femoral nerve, arising from its posterior division (root values L2–L4 via the femoral nerve).
major.saphenous.course: Travels through the adductor (subsartorial) canal with the femoral vessels, and exits the canal before the adductor hiatus to reach the medial side of the leg.
major.saphenous.motor_distribution: None — the saphenous nerve is the terminal cutaneous (sensory) branch of the femoral nerve.
major.saphenous.sensory_distribution: The medial side of the leg and foot.
major.saphenous.clinical_testing: The nerve accompanies the long (great) saphenous vein in the leg and can be damaged during stripping of that vein, causing pain, paraesthesia or complete sensory loss on the medial side of the lower leg.
major.saphenous.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.superior-gluteal.name: Superior gluteal nerve
major.superior-gluteal.root_values: Branch of the sacral plexus; root values L4, L5 and S1.
major.superior-gluteal.course: Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen superior to (above) the piriformis, accompanied by the superior gluteal artery and vein.
major.superior-gluteal.motor_distribution: Gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae.

major.inferior-gluteal.name: Inferior gluteal nerve
major.inferior-gluteal.root_values: Branch of the sacral plexus; root values L5, S1 and S2.
major.inferior-gluteal.course: Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen inferior to (below) the piriformis, accompanied by the inferior gluteal vessels.
verify: clinical_testing: no bedside test or lesion pattern specific to this nerve is stated in the consulted sources; not entered - verify
major.inferior-gluteal.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.sciatic.name: Sciatic nerve
major.sciatic.root_values: From the sacral plexus; root values L4–S3. The largest nerve in the body, about 2 cm wide as a flat band; it consists of two nerves — the tibial and common fibular nerves — bound together in a single connective tissue sheath.
major.sciatic.course: Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, emerging inferior to the piriformis; descends, crossing the posterior surfaces of the superior gemellus, obturator internus, inferior gemellus and quadratus femoris; enters the posterior compartment of the thigh deep to the long head of biceps femoris; and bifurcates at the apex of the popliteal fossa into the tibial and common fibular nerves (in about 12% of people the two divisions separate as they leave the pelvis).
major.sciatic.motor_distribution: Directly: the posterior compartment of the thigh (biceps femoris, semimembranosus and semitendinosus) and the hamstring portion of adductor magnus. Indirectly, via its terminal branches: all the muscles of the leg and foot. The nerve innervates no muscles in the gluteal region.
major.sciatic.sensory_distribution: No direct sensory functions; indirectly, via its terminal branches, it supplies the lateral leg, the heel, and the dorsal and plantar surfaces of the foot.
major.sciatic.clinical_testing: Piriformis syndrome — compression of the nerve by the piriformis muscle — presents with radicular pain, numbness and muscle weakness and buttock tenderness, and the pain may be exacerbated by internal rotation of the lower limb at the hip. Injection safety: the nerve passes through the lower medial quadrant of the gluteal region, so intramuscular injections are made only into the upper lateral quadrant.
major.sciatic.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.tibial.name: Tibial nerve
major.tibial.root_values: Terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; root values L4–S3.
major.tibial.course: Arises at the apex of the popliteal fossa, travels through the fossa and descends in the posterior compartment of the leg, passes posterior and inferior to the medial malleolus through the tarsal tunnel (beneath the flexor retinaculum), and terminates just distal to the tunnel by dividing into the medial and lateral plantar nerves.
major.tibial.motor_distribution: The posterior compartment of the leg — superficial: plantaris, soleus and gastrocnemius; deep: popliteus, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus and tibialis posterior. In the foot, via the medial and lateral plantar branches: the intrinsic muscles of the sole, except extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis (deep fibular nerve).
major.tibial.sensory_distribution: Via the branches that contribute to the sural nerve: the posterolateral leg and the lateral foot. The medial calcaneal branches supply the heel. The medial plantar branch supplies the plantar surface of the medial three and a half digits and the associated sole; the lateral plantar branch the lateral one and a half digits and the associated sole — together, the whole sole of the foot.
major.tibial.clinical_testing: Tarsal tunnel syndrome — entrapment of the nerve in the tarsal tunnel — causes altered sensation in the sole of the foot and, in severe cases, weakness and wasting of the intrinsic muscles of the foot. Damage to the nerve causes loss of plantarflexion and loss of flexion of the toes, and weakened inversion of the foot.
major.tibial.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.common-fibular.name: Common fibular (peroneal) nerve
major.common-fibular.root_values: Terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; root values L4–S2.
major.common-fibular.course: Arises at the apex of the popliteal fossa where the sciatic nerve bifurcates, follows the medial border of biceps femoris inferolaterally across the lateral head of gastrocnemius, wraps around the neck of the fibula between the attachments of fibularis longus, and divides into the superficial fibular and deep fibular nerves.
major.common-fibular.motor_distribution: Directly: the short head of biceps femoris. Via the superficial fibular nerve: the lateral compartment of the leg (fibularis longus and brevis — eversion). Via the deep fibular nerve: the anterior compartment of the leg (tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus and extensor hallucis longus — dorsiflexion and extension of the digits) and some intrinsic muscles of the foot.
major.common-fibular.sensory_distribution: The lateral sural cutaneous branch supplies the upper lateral leg; the sural communicating branch joins the tibial contribution to form the sural nerve (lower posterolateral leg). Via the superficial fibular nerve: the anterolateral leg and the dorsum of the foot except the first web space. Via the deep fibular nerve: the first web space.
major.common-fibular.clinical_testing: The nerve is most commonly damaged at the neck of the fibula, by fracture or by a tight plaster cast: dorsiflexion is lost and the foot is held in plantarflexion — footdrop, with its characteristic gait; eversion and extension of the digits are also lost, with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and the lateral leg, while the medial leg (saphenous territory) and the heel and sole (tibial territory) are preserved.
major.common-fibular.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.superficial-fibular.name: Superficial fibular nerve
major.superficial-fibular.root_values: Terminal division of the common fibular nerve (root values L4–S2 via the common fibular nerve).
major.superficial-fibular.course: Arises where the common fibular nerve divides at the neck of the fibula, and descends within the lateral compartment of the leg.
major.superficial-fibular.motor_distribution: Fibularis (peroneus) longus and fibularis brevis — eversion of the foot.
major.superficial-fibular.sensory_distribution: The anterolateral leg and the dorsum of the foot, except the first web space (deep fibular nerve).
major.superficial-fibular.clinical_testing: Its function is lost in the parent nerve's lesion at the fibular neck: eversion is lost, together with the dorsiflexion supplied by the deep fibular division, in footdrop.
major.superficial-fibular.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.deep-fibular.name: Deep fibular nerve
major.deep-fibular.root_values: Terminal division of the common fibular nerve (root values L4–S2 via the common fibular nerve).
major.deep-fibular.course: Arises where the common fibular nerve divides at the neck of the fibula, and descends within the anterior compartment of the leg.
major.deep-fibular.motor_distribution: The anterior compartment of the leg — tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus and fibularis tertius — and the muscles on the dorsum of the foot, extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis.
major.deep-fibular.sensory_distribution: The web space between the great toe and the second toe (the first web space).
major.deep-fibular.clinical_testing: Anterior compartment syndrome of the leg can damage the deep fibular nerve, resulting in foot drop; a deep fibular palsy can itself produce footdrop.
major.deep-fibular.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.sural.name: Sural nerve
major.sural.root_values: Formed by the union of the medial sural cutaneous nerve (a branch of the tibial nerve) with the fibular communicating branch of the lateral sural cutaneous nerve (from the common fibular nerve); it has no spinal root values of its own.
major.sural.course: Formed in the leg by the union of the medial sural cutaneous nerve with the fibular communicating branch, and descends in the posterior leg.
major.sural.motor_distribution: None — a cutaneous nerve, formed from sensory branches of the tibial and common fibular nerves.
major.sural.sensory_distribution: The posterior surface of the leg and the lateral side of the foot.
verify: clinical_testing: no bedside test or lesion pattern specific to the sural nerve is stated in the consulted sources; not entered - verify
major.sural.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

major.pudendal.name: Pudendal nerve
major.pudendal.root_values: Formed on the posterior pelvic wall from the anterior divisions of the ventral rami of S2, S3 and S4 (sacral plexus).
major.pudendal.course: Descends between the piriformis and ischiococcygeus muscles, leaves the pelvis through the lower part of the greater sciatic foramen, crosses the sacrospinous ligament near the ischial spine, re-enters the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen, and runs with the internal pudendal artery and vein through the pudendal (Alcock's) canal in the fascia over obturator internus, dividing into the inferior rectal nerve, the perineal nerve and the dorsal nerve of the penis or clitoris.
major.pudendal.motor_distribution: Via the perineal nerve: bulbospongiosus, ischiocavernosus, levator ani and the external urethral sphincter; via the inferior rectal nerve: the external anal sphincter — together, the somatic control of urinary and faecal continence.
major.pudendal.sensory_distribution: The external genitalia of both sexes and the skin of the perineum: the perianal skin and the lower third of the anal canal (inferior rectal nerve); the perineum and the labia majora and minora, or the posterior scrotum (perineal nerve); and the skin of the penis or clitoris (dorsal nerve).
major.pudendal.clinical_testing: Clinical procedure — the pudendal nerve block, used to provide analgesia for vaginal childbirth, episiotomy repair and minor vaginal procedures: with the patient in the lithotomy position, the ischial spine is palpated transvaginally and local anaesthetic is injected around the spine, aspirating before injecting because the internal pudendal artery accompanies the nerve.
major.pudendal.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

resp.nasal-cavity.name: Nasal cavity
resp.nasal-cavity.note: the nasal cavity as a space has no concept in the release; geometry links are the nose organ record and its named parts and cartilages
resp.nasal-cavity.extent: The most superior part of the respiratory tract; extends from the vestibule of the nose to the nasopharynx
resp.nasal-cavity.structure: Three divisions: vestibule (around the anterior external opening), respiratory region (ciliated pseudostratified epithelium with mucus-secreting goblet cells) and olfactory region at the apex, lined by olfactory cells with olfactory receptors
resp.nasal-cavity.function: Warms and humidifies inspired air; removes and traps pathogens and particulate matter; sense of smell; drains and clears the paranasal sinuses and lacrimal ducts

resp.nasopharynx.name: Nasopharynx
verify: no BP3D concept: this structure has no concept in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (see the inventory gap analysis); the record is sourced text without geometry
resp.nasopharynx.extent: Between the base of the skull and the soft palate; continuous with the nasal cavity
resp.nasopharynx.structure: Lined with respiratory epithelium (ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells); the posterosuperior wall contains the adenoid (pharyngeal) tonsils, which enlarge between 3-8 years of age and then regress
resp.nasopharynx.function: Respiratory part of the pharynx: conditions inspired air and propagates it towards the larynx

resp.oropharynx.name: Oropharynx
verify: no BP3D concept: this structure has no concept in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (see the inventory gap analysis); the record is sourced text without geometry
resp.oropharynx.extent: The middle part of the pharynx, between the soft palate and the superior border of the epiglottis
resp.oropharynx.structure: Contains the posterior one-third of the tongue, the lingual tonsils, the palatine tonsils (in the tonsillar fossa) and the superior constrictor muscle; with the palatine, adenoid and lingual tonsils it forms part of Waldeyer's ring
resp.oropharynx.function: A passageway shared by air and food; involved in the voluntary and involuntary phases of swallowing

resp.laryngopharynx.name: Laryngopharynx
verify: no BP3D concept: this structure has no concept in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (see the inventory gap analysis); the record is sourced text without geometry
resp.laryngopharynx.extent: The most distal part of the pharynx, between the superior border of the epiglottis and the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage (C6); continuous inferiorly with the oesophagus
resp.laryngopharynx.structure: Lies posterior to the larynx and communicates with it via the laryngeal inlet, lateral to which lie the piriform fossae; contains the middle and inferior pharyngeal constrictors
resp.laryngopharynx.function: Directs air into the larynx and swallowed material into the oesophagus

resp.larynx.name: Larynx
resp.larynx.note: the larynx as an organ has no concept in the release; geometry links are its nine cartilages and its ligament/membrane records as released
resp.larynx.position: Anterior compartment of the neck, suspended from the hyoid bone, spanning C3 to C6; continuous inferiorly with the trachea and opening superiorly into the laryngeal part of the pharynx; oesophagus lies posteriorly
resp.larynx.functions: Phonation, the cough reflex, and protection of the lower respiratory tract
resp.larynx.cartilages: Nine cartilages forming the laryngeal skeleton: three unpaired (epiglottis, thyroid, cricoid) and three paired (arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform)
resp.larynx.cavity_divisions: Supraglottis (inferior surface of epiglottis to the vestibular folds), glottis (the vocal cords and 1 cm below; the opening between the cords is the rima glottidis) and subglottis (to the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage); lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium except the true vocal cords (stratified squamous)
resp.larynx.innervation: Via the vagus nerve: the recurrent laryngeal nerve gives sensory supply to the infraglottis and motor supply to all internal laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid; the superior laryngeal nerve's internal branch is sensory to the supraglottis and its external branch is motor to the cricothyroid
resp.larynx.blood_supply: Superior laryngeal artery (branch of the superior thyroid artery, from the external carotid) and inferior laryngeal artery (branch of the inferior thyroid artery, from the thyrocervical trunk); the superior laryngeal vein drains via the superior thyroid vein to the internal jugular vein, the inferior via the inferior thyroid vein to the left brachiocephalic vein

resp.trachea.name: Trachea
resp.trachea.extent: Arises at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage in the neck as a continuation of the larynx; travels inferiorly into the superior mediastinum, anterior to the oesophagus, and bifurcates at the level of the sternal angle
resp.trachea.structure: Held open by C-shaped cartilage rings (16-20 rings of hyaline cartilage) whose free ends are supported by the trachealis muscle; lined by ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells, forming the mucociliary escalator; at the bifurcation the carina, a ridge of cartilage between the bronchial openings, is the most sensitive area for triggering the cough reflex
resp.trachea.function: Conducts air between the larynx and the main bronchi; the mucociliary escalator traps inhaled particles and pathogens and moves them up out of the airways

resp.main-bronchi.name: Main bronchi
resp.main-bronchi.extent: From the tracheal bifurcation at the sternal angle, each bronchus enters the root of its lung through the hilum
resp.main-bronchi.structure: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left (hence a higher incidence of foreign-body inhalation); the left main bronchus passes inferior to the arch of the aorta and anterior to the thoracic aorta and oesophagus; in the main bronchi, cartilage rings completely encircle the lumen
resp.main-bronchi.function: Deliver air from the trachea to each lung; with branches of the pulmonary artery and veins, the main bronchi make up the roots of the lungs

resp.lobar-bronchi.name: Lobar bronchi
verify: no BP3D concept: this structure has no concept in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (see the inventory gap analysis); the record is sourced text without geometry
resp.lobar-bronchi.note: the release contains no lobar bronchus concept: its bronchial tree jumps from the main bronchi to the segmental bronchial trees
resp.lobar-bronchi.extent: Within the lungs, branching from the main bronchi and dividing into the segmental bronchi
resp.lobar-bronchi.structure: Secondary bronchi; their cartilage is found only in crescent shapes (unlike the complete rings of the main bronchi)
resp.lobar-bronchi.function: One lobar (secondary) bronchus supplies each lobe of the lung: three on the right, two on the left

resp.segmental-bronchi.name: Segmental bronchi

resp.segmental-bronchi.note: geometry links are the release's 21 segmental bronchial tree records (16 lateralised instances and the un-sided lateral, medial, basal and two lingular trees)
resp.segmental-bronchi.extent: Branch from the lobar bronchi within each lobe
resp.segmental-bronchi.structure: Tertiary bronchi; cartilage only in crescent shapes
resp.segmental-bronchi.function: Each segmental bronchus provides air to a bronchopulmonary segment — the functional units of the lungs

resp.bronchioles.name: Bronchioles
verify: no BP3D concept: this structure has no concept in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (see the inventory gap analysis); the record is sourced text without geometry
resp.bronchioles.extent: The segmental bronchi branch repeatedly into numerous smaller bronchioles, ending as terminal bronchioles
resp.bronchioles.structure: The smallest airways: no cartilage and no mucus-secreting goblet cells; club cells produce a surfactant lipoprotein that stops the small airway walls sticking together during expiration; bronchioles are less than 1 mm wide
resp.bronchioles.function: Conducting bronchioles transport air but are not involved in gas exchange; the terminal bronchioles are the last part of the conducting zone

resp.respiratory-bronchioles.function: The first airways at which gas exchange occurs, through their alveolar outpocketings

resp.alveolar-ducts-and-sacs.extent: Respiratory bronchioles branch into alveolar ducts, which open into clusters of alveolar sacs
resp.alveolar-ducts-and-sacs.structure: Ducts opening into clustered sacs of alveoli
resp.alveolar-ducts-and-sacs.function: Conduct air into the alveolar sacs, where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged

resp.alveoli.name: Alveoli

resp.alveoli.extent: At the ends of the respiratory zone throughout the lung parenchyma, extending from the lumens of the respiratory bronchioles and forming the alveolar sacs
resp.alveoli.structure: Tiny air-filled pockets with thin walls of simple squamous epithelium; altogether around 300 million alveoli in the adult lungs
resp.alveoli.function: The sites of gaseous exchange in the lungs, providing a large surface area for exchange

resp.right-lung.name: Right lung
resp.right-lung.lobes: Three lobes: superior, middle and inferior
resp.right-lung.fissures: Two fissures: the oblique fissure, running from the inferior border superoposteriorly to the posterior border, separating the inferior lobe from the middle and superior lobes; and the horizontal fissure, running horizontally from the sternum at the level of the 4th rib to meet the oblique fissure
resp.right-lung.root_hilum: Each lung root contains a bronchus, a pulmonary artery, two pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, the pulmonary plexus of nerves and lymphatic vessels; all enter or leave the lung via the hilum, a wedge-shaped area on the mediastinal surface
resp.right-lung.relations: Cone shaped, with apex projecting above the 1st rib into the floor of the neck and base sitting on the diaphragm (the diaphragmatic concavity is deeper on the right, due to the higher right dome over the liver); medial surface related to the oesophagus, heart, inferior vena cava, superior vena cava and azygos vein
resp.right-lung.blood_supply: Deoxygenated blood by the pulmonary arteries; oxygenated blood leaves via the pulmonary veins (two per lung); an extra nutritive supply to the bronchi, lung roots, visceral pleura and lung tissue comes from the bronchial arteries (from the descending aorta); the right bronchial vein drains into the azygos vein
resp.right-lung.nerve_supply: Derived from the pulmonary plexuses: parasympathetic fibres (vagus) stimulate secretion from the bronchial glands, contraction of bronchial smooth muscle and vasodilation of the pulmonary vessels; sympathetic fibres (sympathetic trunks) stimulate relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle and vasoconstriction of the pulmonary vessels; visceral afferent fibres conduct pain impulses to the sensory ganglion of the vagus nerve

resp.left-lung.name: Left lung
resp.left-lung.fissures: One fissure: the oblique fissure, similar to that of the right lung, separating the superior and inferior lobes
resp.left-lung.root_hilum: Each lung root contains a bronchus, a pulmonary artery, two pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, the pulmonary plexus of nerves and lymphatic vessels; all enter or leave the lung via the hilum, a wedge-shaped area on the mediastinal surface
resp.left-lung.relations: Slightly smaller than the right lung because of the heart; its anterior border is marked by the cardiac notch, a deep notch created by the apex of the heart; medial surface related to the heart, arch of aorta, thoracic aorta and oesophagus; base sits on the diaphragm
resp.left-lung.blood_supply: Deoxygenated blood by the pulmonary arteries; oxygenated blood leaves via the pulmonary veins (two per lung); nutritive supply from the bronchial arteries (from the descending aorta); the left bronchial vein drains into the accessory hemiazygos vein
resp.left-lung.nerve_supply: Derived from the pulmonary plexuses: parasympathetic fibres (vagus) stimulate secretion from the bronchial glands, contraction of bronchial smooth muscle and vasodilation of the pulmonary vessels; sympathetic fibres (sympathetic trunks) stimulate relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle and vasoconstriction of the pulmonary vessels; visceral afferent fibres conduct pain impulses to the sensory ganglion of the vagus nerve

resp.nasal-cavity-organ.name: Nasal cavity (structure)
resp.nasal-cavity-organ.note: companion to the pathway record of the same name: the cavity's own sourced structure; the release carries no nasal cavity concept
resp.nasal-cavity-organ.divisions: Vestibule, respiratory region and olfactory region
resp.nasal-cavity-organ.functions: Warms and humidifies inspired air; removes and traps pathogens and particulate matter; sense of smell; drains and clears the paranasal sinuses and lacrimal ducts
resp.nasal-cavity-organ.conchae_meatuses: Three conchae (inferior, middle, superior) project from the lateral walls, creating four pathways: the inferior meatus (below the inferior concha), middle meatus (between inferior and middle conchae), superior meatus (between middle and superior conchae) and the spheno-ethmoidal recess (above and behind the superior concha); the conchae increase surface area and make airflow slow and turbulent, so air spends longer in contact with the cavity walls
resp.nasal-cavity-organ.openings: Frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoidal sinuses open into the middle meatus at the semilunar hiatus; the middle ethmoidal sinuses empty onto the ethmoidal bulla; the posterior ethmoidal sinuses open at the level of the superior meatus; the sphenoid sinus drains onto the posterior roof; the nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus; the auditory (Eustachian) tube opens into the nasopharynx at the level of the inferior meatus
resp.nasal-cavity-organ.blood_supply: From both carotids: internal carotid via the anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries (branches of the ophthalmic artery, descending through the cribriform plate); external carotid via the sphenopalatine, greater palatine, superior labial and lateral nasal arteries; the branches anastomose, particularly in the anterior nose (Kiesselbach area); veins drain to the pterygoid plexus, facial vein or cavernous sinus
resp.nasal-cavity-organ.innervation: Special sensory (smell) by the olfactory nerves, whose fibres pass through the cribriform plate from the olfactory bulb; general sensory supply to septum and lateral walls by the nasopalatine nerve (maxillary) and nasociliary nerve (ophthalmic); the skin of the external nose by the trigeminal nerve

resp.pharynx.name: Pharynx
verify: no BP3D concept: this structure has no concept in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (see the inventory gap analysis); the record is sourced text without geometry
resp.pharynx.note: the pharynx has no concept in the release (only its subdivision classes, its raphe and its muscles); its muscle records live in the muscular module (superior/middle/inferior constrictors, stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus)
resp.pharynx.extent: A muscular tube connecting the oral and nasal cavities to the larynx and oesophagus; it begins at the base of the skull and ends at the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage (C6)
resp.pharynx.parts: Three parts, superior to inferior: nasopharynx (base of skull to soft palate), oropharynx (soft palate to superior border of the epiglottis) and laryngopharynx (superior border of the epiglottis to the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage, C6)
resp.pharynx.muscles: Two groups: circular muscles — the superior, middle and inferior pharyngeal constrictors, arranged like stacked glasses, contracting sequentially from superior to inferior to propel the bolus into the oesophagus (the inferior constrictor has thyropharyngeal and cricopharyngeal parts); longitudinal muscles — stylopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus, which shorten and widen the pharynx and elevate the larynx during swallowing
resp.pharynx.innervation: Motor and sensory supply mainly via the pharyngeal plexus (pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves, branches of the external laryngeal nerve and sympathetic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion); all pharyngeal muscles are supplied by the vagus except the stylopharyngeus (glossopharyngeal); sensory supply is mainly glossopharyngeal, with the maxillary nerve to the anterior/superior nasopharynx
resp.pharynx.blood_supply: Arterial supply from branches of the external carotid artery: the ascending pharyngeal artery and branches of the facial, lingual and maxillary arteries; venous drainage by the pharyngeal venous plexus into the internal jugular vein

resp.pleura.name: Pleurae and pleural cavities
verify: no BP3D concept: this structure has no concept in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (see the inventory gap analysis); the record is sourced text without geometry

ta_name: ambiguous in TA2 (FIPAT 2nd ed., version 2.07) consulted 2026-11-06 — compound record ('pleurae and pleural cavities'): TA2 terms 3322 pleura and 3316 cavitas pleuralis denote its two parts separately.
resp.pleura.note: no pleura concept of any kind exists in the release; the only pleura-adjacent concepts are the two pulmopleural compartments, censused in the inventory as compartment concepts, not records
resp.pleura.layers: Two pleurae, one associated with each lung; each is a serous membrane (a layer of simple squamous cells — mesothelium — on connective tissue) divided into the visceral pleura, which covers the lungs, and the parietal pleura, which covers the internal surface of the thoracic cavity; the two are continuous with each other at the hilum of the lung
resp.pleura.parietal_parts: The parietal pleura is subdivided by the surface it covers: mediastinal pleura (lateral aspect of the mediastinum), cervical pleura (the extension into the neck), costal pleura (inner aspect of the ribs, costal cartilages and intercostal muscles) and diaphragmatic pleura (superior surface of the diaphragm)
resp.pleura.cavity_and_fluid: The pleural cavity is a potential space between the visceral and parietal pleura containing a small volume of serous fluid; the fluid lubricates the pleural surfaces so they slide over each other, and its surface tension pulls the two layers together, ensuring the lung expands when the thorax expands
resp.pleura.recesses: Two recesses in each pleural cavity where opposing parietal surfaces touch and fluid can collect: the costodiaphragmatic recess (between the costal and diaphragmatic pleurae) and the costomediastinal recess (between the costal and mediastinal pleurae, behind the sternum)
resp.pleura.innervation_supply: The parietal pleura is sensitive to pressure, pain and temperature, producing well-localised pain; it is innervated by the phrenic and intercostal nerves and supplied by the intercostal arteries. The visceral pleura is not sensitive to pain, temperature or touch (its sensory fibres detect stretch only), receives autonomic innervation from the pulmonary plexus, and is supplied by the bronchial arteries

resp.mechanics.name: Respiratory volumes and capacities
verify: no BP3D concept: spirometric values are measurements, not anatomical structures; no geometry is linked by design
ta_name: not found in TA2 (FIPAT 2nd ed., version 2.07) consulted 2026-11-06 — measurements (respiratory volumes and capacities), not an anatomical structure; no TA2 term applies.
resp.mechanics.note: all values are the consulted source's stated approximates, which the source itself notes will vary somewhat between sources; resting adult values. Related structure record: the diaphragm (muscular module, muscle.diaphragm), the dome-shaped muscle at the base of the lungs (S10)

value_definitions.tidal_volume_ml: volume of air taken into the lungs in a resting breath
value_definitions.inspiratory_reserve_volume_ml: reserve that can be inspired beyond a normal inspiration
value_definitions.expiratory_reserve_volume_ml: difference between the lung volume at the end of normal and of maximal expiration
value_definitions.residual_volume_ml: air left in the lungs at the end of maximal expiration, which cannot be voluntarily exhaled
value_definitions.functional_residual_capacity_ml: air left at the end of normal resting expiration (ERV + RV)
value_definitions.vital_capacity_ml: the total usable volume of the lungs under voluntary control
value_definitions.minimal_volume_ml: volume below which the lungs will collapse
value_definitions.anatomical_dead_space_ml: volume of the air-conducting pathways in which no gas exchange occurs (approximately 150 mL in the average adult)
value_definitions.minute_respiratory_volume_ml_per_min: air exchanged in one minute (rate x tidal volume); the source notes the average is closer to 6000
value_definitions.alveolar_ventilation_ml_per_min: (tidal volume - anatomical dead space) x rate, as computed by the source at rest
value_definitions.fev1_percent_of_vital_capacity: volume expired in the first second of a vital capacity determination (FEV1), as a percentage of VC

dig.oral-cavity.name: Oral cavity
dig.oral-cavity.note: the soft palate and uvula records and the gingiva records are inventory records of this module; the palate muscles (levator and tensor veli palatini, uvular muscle) and the jaws are cross-referenced to the muscular and skeletal modules in the inventory
dig.oral-cavity.extent: The mouth (oral or buccal cavity), framed by the cheeks, tongue and palate; it runs from the lips back to the fauces, the opening into the oropharynx
dig.oral-cavity.structure: The lips (covered by the orbicularis oris, the inner lip attached to the gum by the labial frenulum) and the cheeks (buccinator muscles between skin and mucous membrane) form the outer walls; the oral vestibule is the pocket framed inside by the gums and teeth and outside by the cheeks and lips, and the oral cavity proper runs from the gums and teeth to the fauces. Its three accessory structures are the tongue, the salivary glands and the teeth
dig.oral-cavity.function: Ingestion; mechanical digestion by the teeth and tongue, which positions food for chewing, gathers it into a bolus and positions it for swallowing; chemical digestion begins here (salivary amylase and lingual lipase)

dig.oesophagus.name: Oesophagus
dig.oesophagus.extent: A fibromuscular tube approximately 25 cm long, from the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage (C6) to the cardiac orifice of the stomach (T11); it passes through the oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm at T10, and its abdominal portion is approximately 1.25 cm long
dig.oesophagus.structure: Wall of four layers: adventitia (serosa only on the very distal, intraperitoneal part), muscle layer (superior third voluntary striated muscle, middle third mixed, inferior third smooth muscle), submucosa, and mucosa of non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium. Four physiological constrictions: arch of aorta, left main bronchus, cricoid cartilage, diaphragmatic hiatus
dig.oesophagus.function: Conducts the food bolus from the pharynx to the stomach. The upper oesophageal sphincter is an anatomical sphincter of striated muscle (cricopharyngeus), normally constricted to prevent air entering; the lower oesophageal sphincter is a physiological sphincter at the gastro-oesophageal junction (left of T11) that prevents reflux of gastric contents

dig.stomach.name: Stomach
dig.stomach.extent: An intraperitoneal organ between the oesophagus and the duodenum, in the epigastric and left hypochondriac regions; its superior opening (the cardia) is at T11 and the pylorus demarcates the transpyloric plane at L1
dig.stomach.structure: J-shaped, with a long convex greater curvature and a short concave lesser curvature; four divisions: cardia, fundus, body and pylorus (see the Stomach (structure) record)
dig.stomach.function: Receives the bolus from the oesophagus; the pyloric sphincter — an anatomical sphincter of smooth muscle, normally contracted — controls the exit of chyme into the duodenum

dig.duodenum.name: Duodenum
dig.duodenum.extent: The most proximal part of the small intestine, approximately 25 cm long ('twelve fingers length'), running in a C-shape around the head of the pancreas from the pylorus to the duodenojejunal junction
dig.duodenum.structure: Four parts: superior (D1, at L1 — the 'cap'; its first 3 cm are covered by peritoneum on both sides, the remainder retroperitoneal), descending (D2, L1-L3; the major duodenal papilla on its internal wall is the opening of the hepatopancreatic ampulla), inferior (D3, at L3; crosses the IVC and aorta, posterior to the superior mesenteric artery and vein) and ascending (D4, L3-L2; joins the jejunum at the duodenojejunal flexure, whose angle is widened by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum)
dig.duodenum.function: Receives chyme from the stomach and, at the major duodenal papilla, the bile and pancreatic secretions delivered by the hepatopancreatic ampulla; the first part is the most common site of duodenal ulceration

dig.jejunum.name: Jejunum
dig.jejunum.extent: The middle part of the small intestine, beginning at the duodenojejunal flexure; there is no clear external demarcation between the jejunum and the ileum
dig.jejunum.structure: Intraperitoneal, attached to the posterior abdominal wall by the mesentery; located in the upper left quadrant, with a thick intestinal wall, longer vasa recta, fewer arterial arcades and a red colour (the consulted source's distinguishing table against the ileum)
dig.jejunum.function: With the rest of the small intestine (about 6.5 m in the average person), assists in the digestion and absorption of ingested food

dig.ileum.name: Ileum
dig.ileum.note: the ileocecal valve itself has no concept in the release (probe-verified absence); the ileocecal junction concept is the linked geometry
dig.ileum.extent: The distal part of the small intestine, ending at the ileocaecal junction where it meets the large intestine
dig.ileum.structure: Intraperitoneal, attached by the mesentery; located in the lower right quadrant, with a thin intestinal wall, shorter vasa recta, more arterial arcades and a pink colour (the consulted source's distinguishing table against the jejunum)
dig.ileum.function: Assists in the digestion and absorption of ingested food; at the ileocaecal junction the ileum invaginates into the cecum to form the ileocecal valve, whose main function is to prevent reflux of enteric fluid from the colon into the small intestine

dig.cecum-appendix.name: Cecum and appendix
verify: ta_name: ambiguous in TA2 (FIPAT 2nd ed., version 2.07) consulted 2026-11-06 — compound record (two organs in one record): TA2 terms exist separately — 2970 caecum, 2976 appendix vermiformis; no single TA2 term denotes the pair.
dig.cecum-appendix.note: the consulted sources do not describe the structure or function of the appendix itself in the passages used; its inventory record is linked and no unsourced detail is entered
dig.cecum-appendix.extent: The cecum is the first part of the large intestine, receiving the ileum at the ileocaecal junction; the appendix is carried with it in the consulted large-intestine source's division of the large bowel
dig.cecum-appendix.structure: The cecum is a blind-ended pouch: its blind end lies inferiorly and the ascending colon continues from it superiorly
dig.cecum-appendix.function: The ileocaecal valve at the junction separates the small from the large intestine and prevents reflux of enteric fluid from the colon into the small intestine

dig.ascending-colon.name: Ascending colon
dig.ascending-colon.extent: The first of the four parts of the colon (total colon length about 150 cm): retroperitoneal, running superiorly from the cecum on the right side to the right colic (hepatic) flexure at the right lobe of the liver, where it turns 90 degrees
dig.ascending-colon.structure: Carries the colon's distinguishing features: omental appendices (small fat-filled peritoneal pouches), teniae coli (three longitudinal muscle strips — mesocolic, free and omental) and haustra (sacculations produced by teniae contraction); a paracolic gutter lies laterally
dig.ascending-colon.function: As the colon as a whole: absorbs water and electrolytes from the intestinal contents and forms faeces; the ascending colon and proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon are midgut in embryological origin

dig.transverse-colon.name: Transverse colon
dig.transverse-colon.extent: From the right colic (hepatic) flexure to the spleen, where the left colic (splenic) flexure turns 90 degrees inferiorly; attached to the diaphragm by the phrenicocolic ligament; the least fixed part of the colon
dig.transverse-colon.structure: Intraperitoneal, enclosed by the transverse mesocolon; embryologically the proximal two-thirds are midgut and the distal third hindgut; carries teniae coli, haustra and omental appendices
dig.transverse-colon.function: Absorbs water and electrolytes and forms faeces (the colon's function, per the consulted source)

dig.descending-colon.name: Descending colon
dig.descending-colon.extent: From the left colic (splenic) flexure inferiorly; retroperitoneal in most people, lying anterior to the left kidney over its lateral border, then turning medially to become the sigmoid colon
dig.descending-colon.structure: A hindgut part of the colon, carrying teniae coli, haustra and omental appendices; a paracolic gutter lies laterally
dig.descending-colon.function: Absorbs water and electrolytes and forms faeces (the colon's function, per the consulted source)

dig.sigmoid-colon.name: Sigmoid colon
verify: no BP3D concept: this structure has no concept in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (see the inventory gap analysis); the record is sourced text without geometry
dig.sigmoid-colon.note: neither the sigmoid colon nor the sigmoid mesocolon has a concept in the release (probe-verified absences); the TotalSegmentator 'colon' label is one undivided label and does not resolve this gap
dig.sigmoid-colon.extent: Approximately 40 cm long, in the left lower quadrant from the left iliac fossa to the third sacral vertebra (S3), where it becomes the rectum
dig.sigmoid-colon.structure: S-shaped and mobile, suspended by the sigmoid mesocolon; at the rectosigmoid junction the teniae coli broaden out to form a complete longitudinal muscle layer in the rectum, and the haustra and omental appendices cease
dig.sigmoid-colon.function: Absorbs water and electrolytes and forms faeces (the colon's function, per the consulted source); a hindgut part of the colon

dig.rectum.name: Rectum
dig.rectum.extent: The most distal segment of the large intestine: continuous proximally with the sigmoid colon, beginning at S3, and terminating into the anal canal; the most posterior pelvic viscus
dig.rectum.structure: Macroscopically distinct from the colon by the absence of taenia coli, haustra and omental appendices. Three flexure groups: the sacral flexure (following the sacrum and coccyx), the anorectal flexure (formed by puborectalis tone, contributing to continence) and three lateral flexures formed by transverse folds of the internal wall. Peritoneal coverings: superior third anterior and lateral surfaces, middle third anterior only, lower third none
dig.rectum.function: A temporary store for faeces; its final segment, the ampulla, relaxes to accumulate and store faeces before defecation

dig.anal-canal.name: Anal canal
verify: no BP3D concept: this structure has no concept in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (see the inventory gap analysis); the record is sourced text without geometry
dig.anal-canal.note: the anal canal, the anus and the pectinate line have no concepts in the release (probe-verified absences); the external anal sphincter is the muscular module's record (muscle.external-anal-sphincter), censused in this module's inventory as a cross-reference
dig.anal-canal.extent: The final segment of the gastrointestinal tract, approximately 4 cm long, beginning as the continuation of the rectum, passing inferoposteriorly through the pelvic floor to the anus; it lies within the anal triangle of the perineum between the right and left ischioanal fossae
dig.anal-canal.structure: Two sphincters keep the canal collapsed: the internal anal sphincter (involuntary circular smooth muscle surrounding the upper two-thirds) and the external anal sphincter (voluntary, surrounding the lower two-thirds, blending superiorly with puborectalis); their fusion with puborectalis forms the anorectal ring. The superior mucosa is thrown into anal columns joined by anal valves, which collectively form the pectinate (dentate) line dividing the hindgut-derived upper canal from the proctodeum-derived lower canal
dig.anal-canal.function: Defecation and the maintenance of faecal continence; the canal is collapsed by the anal sphincters except during defecation

organ.stomach.name: Stomach (structure)
organ.stomach.note: the cardia, fundus, body and pylorus named here are sourced text: the release carries no stomach-part concepts (probe-verified absences in the inventory). The supplying vessels are cardiovascular module records (e.g. artery.celiac-artery, artery.gastroduodenal-artery) and are not duplicated here
organ.stomach.parts: Four divisions: cardia (surrounds the superior opening of the stomach, at T11), fundus (the rounded, often gas-filled part superior and to the left of the cardia), body (the large central region, inferior to the fundus) and pylorus (pyloric antrum, pyloric canal and pyloric sphincter; the sphincter demarcates the transpyloric plane at L1)
organ.stomach.curvatures: Greater curvature: the long convex lateral border, from the cardiac notch to the pyloric antrum, giving attachment to the greater omentum; supplied by the short gastric and right and left gastro-omental arteries. Lesser curvature: the short concave medial border, where the angular notch marks the junction of body and pyloric part and the hepatogastric ligament attaches; supplied by the left gastric artery and the right gastric branch of the hepatic artery
organ.stomach.sphincters: Inferior oesophageal sphincter at the cardiac orifice (T11; the oesophagus passes the diaphragmatic hiatus at T10) — physiological, not under voluntary control. Pyloric sphincter — anatomical, of smooth muscle, controlling the exit of chyme, normally contracted
organ.stomach.blood_supply: All arterial supply derives from the coeliac trunk and its branches, with anastomoses along both curvatures. The veins parallel the arteries and drain into the hepatic portal system: right and left gastric veins directly to the portal vein, short gastric and left gastro-omental veins to the splenic vein, right gastro-omental vein to the superior mesenteric vein
organ.stomach.innervation: Parasympathetic supply from the anterior and posterior vagal trunks; sympathetic supply from T6-T9 via the greater splanchnic nerve to the coeliac plexus, which also carries pain fibres

organ.liver.name: Liver
organ.liver.note: the quadrate lobe, porta hepatis, bare area and the named ligaments are sourced text: the release carries no concepts for them (probe-verified absences). The supplying vessels are cardiovascular module records (artery.hepatic-artery-proper, artery.common-hepatic-artery, vein.hepatic-portal-vein, vein.hepatic-vein) and are cited, not duplicated. The release also carries a 'hepatovenous segment ix' concept (IS-A only) with no counterpart in the eight-segment Couinaud classification (S13); it is an inventory record and deliberately has no clinical segment record here
organ.liver.position: A peritoneal organ of the right upper quadrant — predominantly the right hypochondrium and epigastrium, extending into the left hypochondrium; the largest visceral structure in the abdominal cavity and the largest gland in the body, an accessory gland of digestion. About 2% of adult body weight (approximately 1400 g in females and 1800 g in males, S13)
organ.liver.surfaces: Diaphragmatic surface (anterosuperior): smooth and convex, fitting beneath the diaphragm; its posterior aspect is not covered by visceral peritoneum and contacts the diaphragm directly — the bare area. Visceral surface (posteroinferior): covered by peritoneum except at the gallbladder fossa and the porta hepatis, and moulded by the right kidney, right adrenal gland, right colic flexure, transverse colon, first part of the duodenum, gallbladder, oesophagus and stomach
organ.liver.lobes: Externally a large right lobe and a smaller left lobe, divided by the falciform ligament. Caudate lobe: on the upper visceral surface, between the IVC and the fossa for the ligamentum venosum. Quadrate lobe: on the lower visceral surface, between the gallbladder and the fossa for the ligamentum teres. The functional (Couinaud) division into eight segments is carried in this module's segment records
organ.liver.ligaments: Falciform ligament: anterior surface to the anterior abdominal wall, its free edge containing the ligamentum teres (remnant of the umbilical vein). Coronary ligament: superior surface to the diaphragm, demarcating the bare area. Right and left triangular ligaments: the unions of the coronary folds at each lobe. Lesser omentum: to the lesser curvature of the stomach and the first part of the duodenum; its hepatoduodenal ligament surrounds the portal triad
organ.liver.blood_supply: Dual supply: the hepatic artery proper contributes approximately 25% of the liver's blood (oxygenated, from the coeliac trunk) and the hepatic portal vein approximately 75% (nutrient-rich blood from the gut; the portal vein is formed by the union of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins, S13). Drainage is by the hepatic veins into the IVC
organ.liver.nerve_supply: The hepatic plexus (sympathetic fibres from the coeliac plexus and parasympathetic fibres from the vagus) enters at the porta hepatis and follows the hepatic artery and portal vein branches; Glisson's capsule is supplied by the lower intercostal nerves, so capsular distension gives sharp, localised pain

organ.gallbladder.name: Gallbladder
organ.gallbladder.position_relations: An intraperitoneal, pear-shaped sac in the right hypochondrium, lying in a fossa between the inferior aspects of the right and quadrate lobes of the liver, anterior to the first part of the duodenum; posterior relations are the transverse colon and proximal duodenum
organ.gallbladder.parts: Fundus: the rounded distal end, projecting at the inferior border of the liver in the mid-clavicular line. Body: the largest part. Neck: tapers into the cystic duct and contains a mucosal fold (Hartmann's pouch), a common site for gallstones to lodge
organ.gallbladder.function: Concentrates and stores the bile produced by the liver (capacity 30-50 mL); bile is released into the biliary tree in response to cholecystokinin
organ.gallbladder.blood_supply: The cystic artery, a branch of the right hepatic artery (from the common hepatic artery, from the coeliac trunk). Venous drainage: the neck via cystic veins directly into the portal vein; the fundus and body into the hepatic sinusoids
organ.gallbladder.innervation: Coeliac plexus (sympathetic and sensory fibres) and the vagus nerve (parasympathetic; gallbladder contraction and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi), although most post-prandial emptying is driven by cholecystokinin

organ.pancreas.name: Pancreas
verify: no BP3D concept: the head, neck, body, tail and uncinate process named in the parts field have no concepts in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (probe-verified absences); the parts are sourced text and the record's geometry is the whole-organ pancreas record
organ.pancreas.note: the supplying vessels are cardiovascular module records (artery.splenic-artery, artery.gastroduodenal-artery, artery.superior-mesenteric-artery, vein.splenic-vein) and are cited, not duplicated
organ.pancreas.position: In the upper abdomen at the transpyloric plane (L1), deep in the epigastric and left hypochondriac regions; retroperitoneal except for the tail
organ.pancreas.parts: Five parts: head (the widest part, sitting in the C-curve of the duodenum), uncinate process (a hook from the lower head extending medially beneath the body, posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels), neck (between head and body, overlying the superior mesenteric vessels and the formation of the portal vein), body (crossing the midline posterior to the stomach) and tail (the left-most part, the only intraperitoneal part, reaching the splenic hilum within the splenorenal ligament with the splenic vessels)
organ.pancreas.duct_system: The main pancreatic duct runs the length of the gland (collecting from intercalated and intralobular ducts draining about one million acini) and unites with the common bile duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla of Vater, opening into the second part of the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla; the sphincter of Oddi surrounds the ampulla. The consulted source does not describe an accessory pancreatic duct
organ.pancreas.blood_supply: Pancreatic branches of the splenic artery; the head is additionally supplied by the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (gastroduodenal, from the coeliac trunk) and the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (superior mesenteric artery). Venous drainage: head to superior mesenteric branches of the hepatic portal vein, the remainder to the splenic vein

seg.couinaud-i.sector: The caudate lobe: outside the functional right / left division of the liver (the functional left lobe is segments II-IV and the functional right lobe segments V-VIII)
seg.couinaud-i.position: Located posteriorly (S13). Autonomous: it receives blood from both the right and left hepatic artery and portal branches, drains bile into both the right and left hepatic ducts, and has independent venous drainage directly into the IVC (S14)
seg.couinaud-i.definition: One of the eight independent functional segments of the Couinaud classification: each segment has its own portal pedicle — a hepatic arterial branch, a portal branch and a bile duct — with a separate hepatic venous branch providing outflow (S13). dig.biliary-tree.name: Biliary tree
verify: no BP3D concept: the common bile duct named in the sequence has no concept in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (probe-verified absence); the release's extrahepatic tree runs from the common hepatic duct and the cystic duct with the final common channel unnamed
no BP3D concept: the hepatopancreatic ampulla and the major duodenal papilla named in the sequence and termination have no concepts in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (probe-verified absences)

ta_name: ambiguous in TA2 (FIPAT 2nd ed., version 2.07) consulted 2026-11-06 — collective record: TA2 names the parts separately (3064 ductus biliferi interlobulares, 3091 ductus biliares extrahepatici, 3092 ductus hepaticus communis, 3101 ductus cysticus, 3103 ductus biliaris) and has no single term for the whole biliary tree.
dig.biliary-tree.note: the cystic artery and the hepatic arterial and portal records relevant to this system are cardiovascular module records and are cited, not duplicated
dig.biliary-tree.sequence: Bile secreted by the hepatocytes drains through canaliculi, intralobular ducts and collecting ducts into the left and right hepatic ducts, which converge to form the common hepatic duct; the cystic duct (the duct to and from the gallbladder) joins it to form the common bile duct, which descends posterior to the first part of the duodenum and the head of the pancreas, is joined by the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater) and empties into the duodenum
dig.biliary-tree.territory: Both lobes of the liver, drained by the right and left hepatic ducts and their intrahepatic trees; the gallbladder is a side reservoir on the cystic duct, concentrating and storing bile between meals
dig.biliary-tree.termination: The major duodenal papilla, in the second part of the duodenum; flow is regulated by the sphincter of Oddi, which surrounds the hepatopancreatic ampulla

dig.oral-cavity-structure.name: Oral cavity (structure)
dig.oral-cavity-structure.note: the hard palate and the palatine tonsil named here have no concepts in the release (probe-verified absences); the maxilla and palatine bones are skeletal module records
dig.oral-cavity-structure.divisions: Oral vestibule: the pocket framed inside by the gums and teeth and outside by the cheeks and lips. Oral cavity proper: from the gums and teeth back to the fauces, the opening between the oral cavity and the oropharynx (throat)
dig.oral-cavity-structure.palate: Hard palate (anterior): formed by the maxillary and palatine bones, a wall between the oral and nasal cavities and a rigid shelf against which the tongue forces food during chewing. Soft palate (posterior): mainly skeletal muscle, with the uvula dropping from the centre of its posterior edge; on swallowing the soft palate and uvula move up to block the nasal cavity. The palatoglossal arch (front) and palatopharyngeal arch (behind) extend down from the soft palate, with the palatine tonsils between them and the lingual tonsils at the base of the tongue
dig.oral-cavity-structure.functions: The tongue facilitates ingestion, mechanical digestion, chemical digestion (lingual lipase), sensation (including taste, via the taste buds of the fungiform papillae), swallowing and vocalisation; the cavity receives food and begins its digestion

dig.salivary-glands.name: Salivary glands
verify: no BP3D concept: the parotid gland and the parotid duct described in this record have no concepts in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (probe-verified absences); the release's salivary census carries only the submandibular and sublingual glands
dig.salivary-glands.note: the submandibular duct is the most calculus-susceptible of the salivary ducts (about 80% of salivary calculi, S11)
dig.salivary-glands.major_glands: Three pairs of major glands, lying outside the oral mucosa and each secreting through one central duct: parotid (largest), submandibular (second largest) and sublingual (smallest). Many minor glands (labial, buccal, palatal and lingual) in the mucosa of the mouth and tongue secrete constantly, even in sleep
dig.salivary-glands.parotid: The largest salivary gland, lying between the skin and the masseter near the ear; lobulated, its superficial and deep lobes separated by the facial nerve. It produces serous (watery, enzyme-rich) saliva, transported by the parotid (Stensen) duct, which opens into the oral cavity opposite the maxillary second molar tooth
dig.salivary-glands.submandibular: Bilateral glands in the anterior part of the submandibular triangle, of elongate flattened hook shape with superficial and deep arms; they produce mixed serous and mucous secretions. The submandibular (Wharton) duct, about 5 cm long, emerges anteromedially from the deep arm between the mylohyoid, hyoglossus and genioglossus and opens into the floor of the oral cavity near the frenulum of the tongue. Supplied by the submental artery (branch of the facial artery) and the sublingual artery (branch of the lingual artery)
dig.salivary-glands.sublingual: The smallest of the major glands, below the tongue; it drains into the floor of the oral cavity by the lesser sublingual ducts and Bartholin's duct. Its secretion is mostly mucous — the thickest saliva of the three glands, with the least amylase
dig.salivary-glands.saliva: 1-1.5 litres of saliva are produced per day; saliva is 99.4% water, with salivary amylase initiating carbohydrate breakdown (acting until inactivated by stomach acid), bicarbonate and phosphate buffers keeping pH between 6.35 and 6.85, mucus for lubrication, and IgA and lysozyme for antimicrobial action

dig.dentition.name: Dentition
