dig.dentition.note: the clinical permanent count of 32 includes the four third molars (wisdom teeth); the release carries no third-molar concepts, so its 28 tooth records are the clinical 32 minus the third molars. Deciduous (primary) teeth have no concepts in the release either

value_definitions.permanent_teeth_total: permanent (secondary) teeth in the complete adult dentition (S12)
value_definitions.deciduous_teeth_total: deciduous teeth of the first dentition, appearing from about 6 months and replaced between about 6 and 12 years (S12)
value_definitions.molars: permanent molars, for crushing, including the four third molars (S12)
value_definitions.third_molars_within_molars: the third molars (wisdom teeth) within the molar count; eruption is often delayed and they may remain impacted (S12)
value_definitions.release_permanent_tooth_records: lateralised permanent-tooth records in this module's inventory (counted from digestive-inventory.json); the release models seven tooth types per quadrant, without third molars

dig.peritoneum.name: Peritoneum
verify: no BP3D concept: the parietal peritoneum has no separate concept in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (probe-verified absence); the release carries the peritoneum and the visceral peritoneum only
no BP3D concept: the greater and lesser omenta and the sigmoid mesocolon named in the reflections field have no concepts in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (probe-verified absences)
dig.peritoneum.layers: A continuous membrane of mesothelium (simple squamous epithelium) in two layers. Parietal peritoneum: lines the abdominopelvic wall, derived from somatic mesoderm, with the same somatic nerve supply as the wall it lines — sensitive to pressure, pain, laceration and temperature, with well-localised pain. Visceral peritoneum: covers the viscera, derived from splanchnic mesoderm, with the autonomic supply of the viscus it covers — sensitive only to stretch and chemical irritation, with poorly localised pain referred to the dermatomes of the supplying spinal cord segments
dig.peritoneum.cavity: The peritoneal cavity is the potential space between the parietal and visceral layers, normally containing only a thin film of peritoneal fluid (water, electrolytes, leukocytes and antibodies) that lubricates the movement of the viscera (see the Peritoneal cavity record)
dig.peritoneum.reflections: A mesentery is a double layer of visceral peritoneum connecting an intraperitoneal organ to (usually) the posterior abdominal wall, providing a pathway for nerves, vessels and lymphatics; the small-intestine mesentery is simply 'the mesentery', the others being named (transverse mesocolon, sigmoid mesocolon, mesoappendix). The greater omentum is four layers of visceral peritoneum descending from the greater curvature of the stomach and proximal duodenum and folding back to the transverse colon ('abdominal policeman', with an immunity role). The lesser omentum is a double layer from the lesser curvature and proximal duodenum to the liver: the hepatogastric ligament and the hepatoduodenal ligament, whose free edge contains the portal triad
dig.peritoneum.organ_relations: Intraperitoneal organs are enveloped by visceral peritoneum (stomach, liver and spleen among them). Retroperitoneal organs are covered only on their anterior surface: primarily retroperitoneal (oesophagus, rectum, kidneys among them) and secondarily retroperitoneal, whose mesentery has fused to the posterior wall (ascending and descending colon; also duodenum except its proximal cap and pancreas except its tail)

dig.peritoneal-cavity.name: Peritoneal cavity
verify: no BP3D concept: the peritoneal cavity as a space, the lesser sac, the epiploic foramen and the pelvic pouches named here have no concepts in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (probe-verified absences); the linked geometry is the release's peritoneal sac and peritoneum records
dig.peritoneal-cavity.greater_sac: The greater sac comprises the majority of the peritoneal cavity and is divided by the transverse mesocolon into a supracolic compartment (containing the stomach, liver and spleen) and an infracolic compartment (containing the small intestine and the ascending and descending colon, itself divided into left and right infracolic spaces by the mesentery of the small intestine); the two compartments are connected by the paracolic gutters
dig.peritoneal-cavity.lesser_sac: The lesser sac (omental bursa) lies posterior to the stomach and the lesser omentum and allows the stomach to move freely against the structures posterior and inferior to it; it communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen (of Winslow), situated posterior to the free edge of the lesser omentum (the hepatoduodenal ligament)
dig.peritoneal-cavity.pelvic_pouches: In males the most distal part of the cavity is the rectovesical pouch and the cavity is completely closed. In females there are the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) and the vesicouterine pouch, and the cavity is not completely closed: the uterine tubes open into it

organ.kidney.name: Kidney
verify: internal_structure: no BP3D concept exists for any internal kidney structure (cortex, medulla, pyramid, papilla, column, pelvis, calyx — 74-probe gap analysis in the inventory); the fields are sourced text on the two whole-kidney geometry records
organ.kidney.note: The adrenal (suprarenal) glands sit immediately superior to the kidneys within a separate envelope of the renal fascia (S1). The source release files them under the endocrine system, not this module — see the inventory's adrenal_filing finding; they are endocrine module records, cross-referenced, never duplicated here. The renal vessels are cardiovascular module records, cited per field.
organ.kidney.position: Bilateral bean-shaped organs, reddish-brown, in the posterior abdomen; they lie retroperitoneally either side of the vertebral column, typically extending from T12 to L3, the right kidney often slightly lower due to the presence of the liver; each kidney is approximately three vertebrae in length.
organ.kidney.coverings: Deep to superficial: (1) renal capsule — a tough fibrous capsule; (2) perirenal fat — a collection of extraperitoneal fat; (3) renal fascia (Gerota's fascia) — encloses the kidneys and the suprarenal glands; (4) pararenal fat — mainly on the posterolateral aspect of the kidney.
organ.kidney.internal_structure: The renal parenchyma divides into an outer cortex and an inner medulla. The cortex extends into the medulla (the renal columns), dividing it into triangular renal pyramids and separating the pyramids and renal papillae; the columns and pyramids together divide the kidney into 6-8 lobes. The apex of each pyramid is a renal papilla, and the papillae are bundles of collecting ducts that transport urine made by the nephrons to the calyces.
organ.kidney.drainage_sequence: Renal papilla -> minor calyx (each papilla is associated with a minor calyx, which collects urine from the pyramid) -> major calyx (several minor calices merge) -> renal pelvis (the flattened, funnel-shaped expansion formed from the major and minor calyces within the hilum) -> ureter.
organ.kidney.hilum: A deep fissure on the medial margin of each kidney, the gateway into the organ: normally the renal vessels and the ureter enter and exit via the hilum. The renal veins leave the hilum anteriorly to the renal arteries.
organ.kidney.arterial_supply: Via the renal arteries (cardiovascular module records artery.renal-artery), arising directly from the abdominal aorta immediately distal to the origin of the superior mesenteric artery; the right renal artery is longer and crosses the inferior vena cava posteriorly. At the hilum the artery forms an anterior division (75% of supply) and a posterior division (25%), from which five segmental arteries originate; the segmental branches are end arteries with no communication between vessels. Intrarenal sequence: segmental -> interlobar (either side of every pyramid) -> arcuate -> interlobular -> afferent arteriole -> glomerulus -> efferent arteriole. Accessory renal arteries are common (in about 25% of patients).
organ.kidney.venous_drainage: Via the left and right renal veins (cardiovascular module record vein.renal-vein), leaving the hilum anterior to the renal arteries and emptying directly into the inferior vena cava; the left renal vein is longer and travels anterior to the abdominal aorta below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery.
organ.kidney.lymphatics: Lymph from the kidney drains into the lateral aortic (para-aortic) lymph nodes, located at the origin of the renal arteries.
organ.kidney.relations: Anterior — left kidney: suprarenal gland, spleen, stomach, pancreas, left colic flexure, jejunum; right kidney: suprarenal gland, liver, duodenum, right colic flexure. Posterior — both: diaphragm, psoas major, quadratus lumborum, transversus abdominis, and the subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves; the left kidney also the 11th and 12th ribs, the right kidney the 12th rib.

structure.nephron.name: Nephron
verify: no BP3D concept: this structure has no concept in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (see the inventory gap analysis); the record is sourced text without geometry — no nephron, glomerulus, capsule, tubule segment or collecting duct concept exists; the record links the two whole-kidney records it would subdivide

ta_name: not found in TA2 (FIPAT 2nd ed., version 2.07) consulted 2026-11-06 — the string 'nephron' occurs in no TA2 term, synonym or related term in the consulted table; TA2 2.07 carries no nephron term.
structure.nephron.note: The nephron is the load-bearing microscopic unit for the physiology follow-on: its segment order here is the sequence a renal compartment model must follow.
structure.nephron.definition: The functional unit of the kidney: a renal corpuscle and a specialised tubule, with its own blood supply. Nephrons cleanse the blood of toxins and balance the constituents of the circulation to homeostatic set points through filtration, reabsorption and secretion; the filtrate they modify becomes urine.
segments_in_order: renal corpuscle (glomerulus within the glomerular capsule)
loop of Henle (descending and ascending limbs)
collecting duct (a common duct shared by many nephrons, draining to the renal papilla)
structure.nephron.corpuscle: The glomerulus is a high-pressure capillary bed of fenestrated capillaries between the afferent and efferent arterioles. The glomerular (Bowman's) capsule surrounds it, captures the filtrate and directs it to the PCT; glomerulus and capsule together form the renal corpuscle.
structure.nephron.types: All glomeruli lie in the cortex. Cortical nephrons have short loops of Henle that do not dip far beyond the cortex; about 15 percent of nephrons are juxtamedullary, with very long loops extending deep into the medulla. Blood exits the glomerulus into the efferent arteriole, which forms the peritubular capillary network around the tubule; for juxtamedullary nephrons the straight capillary portion following the loop deep into the medulla is the vasa recta.
structure.nephron.juxtaglomerular_apparatus: Lying just outside the glomerular capsule: where the afferent and efferent arterioles enter and leave the capsule, the initial part of the DCT comes into direct contact with the arterioles, and the DCT wall there forms the macula densa, a part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA).

organ.ureter.name: Ureter
verify: constrictions: no BP3D concept exists for any ureteric junction, part or orifice (probe-verified); the constrictions are sourced text on the two whole-ureter geometry records
organ.ureter.extent: Two muscular tubes, one draining each kidney. Length as consulted: approximately 25 cm (S2); OpenStax gives approximately 30 cm (S4). The consulted sources differ, so the recorded extent is the range 25-30 cm.
organ.ureter.course: Arises in the abdomen as a continuation of the renal pelvis; the point at which the pelvis narrows to form the ureter is the ureteropelvic junction. Abdominal part: descends on the anterior surface of the psoas major, retroperitoneal throughout. At the sacroiliac joints it crosses the pelvic brim (crossing the bifurcation of the common iliac arteries) and enters the pelvic cavity. Pelvic part: travels down the lateral pelvic walls; at the level of the ischial spines it turns anteromedially towards the bladder and pierces the bladder wall obliquely — a one-way valve (a physiological rather than anatomical sphincter) that prevents reflux of urine into the ureter. Urine is propelled by waves of peristalsis, not passive drainage.
constrictions: ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) — where the renal pelvis narrows to become the ureter
pelvic inlet — where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim
ureterovesical junction (UVJ) — where the ureter enters the bladder; the narrowest of the three
organ.ureter.constriction_note: The three narrowings are the historically taught sites of ureteric calculus obstruction; more recent radiological and clinical evidence suggests stone impaction occurs predominantly at the upper ureter and the ureterovesical junction (S2).
organ.ureter.arterial_supply: Abdominal part: renal artery, testicular/ovarian artery, and ureteral branches directly from the abdominal aorta. Pelvic part: superior and inferior vesical arteries. Venous drainage is by vessels corresponding to the arteries.
organ.ureter.innervation: Via the renal, testicular/ovarian and hypogastric plexuses. Sensory fibres enter the spinal cord at T11-L2, with ureteric pain referred to those dermatomal areas.
organ.ureter.relations_at_risk: Female: at the pelvic brim the ureter lies close to the ovaries (at risk in oophorectomy); about 2 cm superior to the ischial spine it runs underneath the uterine artery ('water under the bridge' — at risk in hysterectomy). Male: the vas deferens crosses the ureter anteriorly. The ureters must be identified during pelvic surgery to avoid accidental damage.

pathway.urinary-pathway.name: Urinary pathway
verify: sequence: the intrarenal stations (papilla, minor and major calyx, renal pelvis) have no BP3D concepts (probe-verified); the pathway is sourced text linking the six whole-organ geometry records
ta_name: not found in TA2 (FIPAT 2nd ed., version 2.07) consulted 2026-11-06 — project pathway construct (the urine pathway as a route, not a structure); TA2 names its organs individually.
pathway.urinary-pathway.function: Urine formed by the nephrons drains from the collecting ducts at the renal papillae into the minor calyces, which merge into the major calyces and the funnel-shaped renal pelvis in the hilum; the pelvis funnels urine by peristalsis into the ureter, which propels it to the bladder, where it is stored until micturition expels it through the urethra.

organ.urinary-bladder.name: Urinary bladder
verify: parts: no BP3D concept exists for any bladder part or feature (apex, body, fundus, neck, trigone, detrusor — probe-verified); the fields are sourced text on the single whole-bladder geometry record

vasculature: no vesical artery or vein has a BP3D concept ('vesical artery'/'vesical vein' probes return zero hits) and the cardiovascular census carries no vesical record; the supply is sourced text (S3) only
organ.urinary-bladder.position: A pelvic organ posterior to the pubic bone and anterior to the rectum; in females it lies anterior to the uterus, in males the prostate lies inferior to it. It is partially retroperitoneal: only its dome carries a peritoneal covering, which projects into the abdomen when the bladder is distended. When full it is oval; when empty it is flattened by the overlying bowel.
organ.urinary-bladder.function: Two roles: temporary storage of urine — a hollow organ with distensible walls and a folded internal lining (rugae) — and assistance in the expulsion of urine, its musculature contracting during micturition with concomitant relaxation of the sphincters.
organ.urinary-bladder.capacity: 400-600 mL in healthy adults (S3); OpenStax gives adult volumes ranging to 500-600 mL (S4).
parts: apex — located superiorly, pointing towards the pubic symphysis; connected to the umbilicus by the median umbilical ligament, a remnant of the urachus
body — the main part of the bladder, between the apex and the fundus
fundus (base) — located posteriorly, triangular-shaped with the tip of the triangle pointing backwards
neck — formed by the convergence of the fundus and the two inferolateral surfaces; continuous with the urethra
organ.urinary-bladder.trigone: A triangular area within the fundus marked by the three orifices: the two ureteric orifices (urine enters from the ureters) and the internal urethral orifice (urine exits). Unlike the rest of the internal bladder, the trigone has smooth walls, explained by its different embryological origin — it develops by the integration of the two mesonephric ducts at the base of the bladder.
organ.urinary-bladder.musculature: The bladder wall's specialised smooth muscle is the detrusor: irregular crisscrossing bands whose fibres run in all directions, retaining structural integrity when stretched and reducing the size of the organ when it empties. The interior surface is transitional epithelium, suited to the bladder's large volume fluctuations. Detrusor fibres often become hypertrophic (prominent trabeculae) when bladder emptying workload increases.
organ.urinary-bladder.vasculature: Primarily derived from the internal iliac vessels. Arterial supply via the superior vesical branch of the internal iliac artery, supplemented in males by the inferior vesical artery and in females by the vaginal arteries (the obturator and inferior gluteal arteries may contribute small branches). Venous drainage by the vesical venous plexus into the internal iliac veins. Lymphatics: the superolateral aspect drains to the external iliac nodes; the neck and fundus drain to the internal iliac, sacral and common iliac nodes.
organ.urinary-bladder.innervation: Sympathetic — hypogastric nerve (T12-L2): relaxes the detrusor, promoting urine retention. Parasympathetic — pelvic nerve (S2-S4): contracts the detrusor, stimulating micturition. Somatic — pudendal nerve (S2-S4): supplies the external urethral sphincter, giving voluntary control. Sensory nerves in the bladder wall report filling to the brain.

structure.urethra.name: Urethra
verify: female: no BP3D concept — the release carries a single unsexed, undivided urethra (probes for 'male urethra', 'female urethra' and every named part return zero hits); the sexed anatomy is sourced text on the one urethra geometry record
male: no BP3D concept — as for female: no sexed form and no prostatic/membranous/spongy part exists in the release
structure.urethra.note: The inventory's single urethra record is unsexed because the source release is; this record states the sex difference from the consulted sources and flags that neither sex's urethra has geometry of its own.
structure.urethra.function: Transports urine from the bladder to the outside of the body for disposal. It is the only urologic organ that shows any significant anatomic difference between males and females; all other urine transport structures are identical. In the male it also transports semen.
structure.urethra.female: Short — about 4 cm. The external urethral orifice is embedded in the anterior vaginal wall, inferior to the clitoris, superior to the vaginal opening (introitus) and medial to the labia minora. Its short length is less of a barrier to fecal bacteria than the longer male urethra — the best explanation for the greater incidence of urinary tract infection in women.
structure.urethra.male: Averages 20 cm, in four regions in order: (1) preprostatic urethra — very short, incorporated into the bladder wall; (2) prostatic urethra — passes through the prostate gland immediately inferior to the bladder, receiving sperm via the ejaculatory ducts and secretions from the seminal vesicles; (3) membranous urethra — passes through the deep muscles of the perineum, invested by the urethral sphincters; (4) spongy (penile) urethra — passes through the corpus spongiosum and exits at the external urethral orifice at the tip of the penis.
structure.urethra.sphincters: Internal urethral sphincter — smooth muscle under involuntary autonomic control at the bladder neck: in males, circular smooth fibres thought to prevent seminal regurgitation during ejaculation; in females, a functional sphincter formed by the anatomy of the bladder neck and proximal urethra (no sphincteric muscle present). External urethral sphincter — skeletal muscle under voluntary control, of the same structure in both sexes, innervated by the pudendal nerve (S2-S4); in males its mechanism is more complex, correlating with fibres of the rectourethralis and levator ani.
structure.urethra.epithelium: In both sexes the proximal urethra is lined by transitional epithelium and the terminal portion by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium; in the male, pseudostratified columnar epithelium lines the urethra between these two.

organ.spleen.name: Spleen
verify: relations: no value asserted — the consulted TeachMeAnatomy page's relations table did not render in the fetched text, and no other consulted source states the spleen's relations; the field stays null rather than unsourced
organ.spleen.note: The release's only intraperitoneal lymphoid organ and, with the thymus, one of only two lymphatic organs it carries at all.
organ.spleen.position: The spleen lies in the upper left quadrant of the abdomen, under the diaphragm and the ribcage; it is not normally palpable (S1). It is intraperitoneal except at its hilum (S1), and is about 12 cm long, attached to the lateral border of the stomach by the gastrosplenic ligament (S2, S1).
organ.spleen.internal_structure: An oval organ with a weak capsule (S1), a diaphragmatic surface against the diaphragm and a visceral surface carrying the hilum, with notches on its anterior and superior borders (S1). Internally, the red pulp filters the blood that passes through it, and the white pulp — lymphoid tissue arranged around a central arteriole — mounts the adaptive immune responses (S2). The release carries no concept for the pulp, the hilum or any other part of the spleen (probe-verified), so this structure is sourced text on the whole-organ record.
organ.spleen.function: The spleen filters the blood, removing old red blood cells, and carries cell-mediated and humoral immune roles (S1); its red pulp is the filtration tissue and its white pulp the adaptive-response tissue (S2). It is fragile — it has no strong capsule (S2) — and its arterial tree divides into vascular segments, which is what makes subtotal splenectomy possible (S1).
organ.spleen.arterial_supply: The splenic artery — the cardiovascular module's record artery.splenic-artery — arises from the coeliac trunk, runs along the superior border of the pancreas within the splenorenal ligament, and divides into five terminal branches with no anastomoses between them, defining the spleen's vascular segments (S1).
organ.spleen.venous_drainage: The splenic vein — the cardiovascular module's record vein.splenic-vein — leaves the hilum and joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the hepatic portal vein (S1).
organ.spleen.lymphatic_drainage: Lymph follows the splenic vessels to the pancreaticosplenic lymph nodes and onward to the coeliac nodes (S1). Neither node group exists as a concept in the release (probe-verified), so this drainage is sourced text only.
organ.spleen.innervation: Sympathetic supply reaches the spleen from the coeliac plexus (S1).

organ.thymus.name: Thymus
verify: arterial_supply: no value asserted — none of the sources consulted in this session states the thymus's arterial supply; the field stays null rather than unsourced
organ.thymus.note: The release carries the thymus as an organ only in the PART-OF table, filed under the contents of the anterior mediastinum; the IS-A table carries only its lobe line.
organ.thymus.position: A bilobed organ lying in the anterior mediastinum, between the sternum and the aorta (S2); more precisely in the superior and retrosternal mediastinum, its two lobes converging at the manubrium, with extensions that can reach the neck toward the thyroid (S3). It develops from the ventral third pharyngeal pouch (S3).
organ.thymus.structure: The thymus is enclosed in a capsule whose trabeculae divide it into lobules; each lobule has a cortex densely packed with thymocytes and a less densely populated medulla (S2). The release carries the organ and its two lobes only — no lobule, cortex or medulla concept exists (probe-verified).
organ.thymus.function: A primary lymphoid organ: the thymus is where T cells (thymocytes) mature, as bone marrow is where B cells mature (S2).
organ.thymus.age_changes: Thymic involution begins after puberty: thymic tissue is lost at roughly 3% per year until about age 35–45, then at roughly 1% per year (S2).

pathway.lymphatic-drainage.name: Lymphatic drainage pathway
verify: no BP3D 4.0 concept exists for this structure (probe-verified over all six release tables by tools/lymph_map.py); the record is sourced text only and links no geometry — this holds for every station of the pathway: no capillary, vessel, trunk or duct of the lymphatic system exists in the release, and the thoracic duct's absence was already probe-verified by Milestone 5 against the same tables
ta_name: not found in TA2 (FIPAT 2nd ed., version 2.07) consulted 2026-11-06 — project pathway construct (a drainage route, not a structure); no TA2 term denotes it.
pathway.lymphatic-drainage.note: The pathway is the system the dataset does not carry: it exists here as sourced clinical text only, in the order the consulted source gives.
sequence: lymphatic capillaries — blind-ended terminal lymphatics in the tissues, where lymph forms
lymphatic vessels — valved collecting vessels, bead-like where their valves constrict them; lymph passes through lymph nodes along the way
lymphatic trunks — the great collecting trunks of the body regions
collecting ducts — the right lymphatic duct and the thoracic duct
the subclavian vein at the junction of the jugular and subclavian veins, where lymph re-enters the blood
pathway.lymphatic-drainage.function: About 20 litres of plasma are filtered out of the blood each day; about 17 litres are reabsorbed and the remaining roughly 3 litres become lymph, which this pathway returns to the venous blood (S2). The system has no central pump: lymph is moved by skeletal muscle action and breathing, and one-way valves prevent backflow (S2). Superficial lymphatics follow the veins and deep lymphatics follow the arteries (S2).
pathway.lymphatic-drainage.ducts_and_territories: The right lymphatic duct drains the right side of the head, the right thorax and the right upper limb into the right subclavian vein. The thoracic duct drains everything else into the left subclavian vein; it begins just beneath the diaphragm in the cisterna chyli, which receives the right and left lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk (S2). In the small intestine, specialised lymphatics — the lacteals — carry the milky fat-laden lymph called chyle (S2).

structure.lymph-nodes.name: Lymph nodes and lymphoid tissue
verify: no BP3D 4.0 concept exists for this structure (probe-verified over all six release tables by tools/lymph_map.py); the record is sourced text only and links no geometry — no lymph node, tonsil or MALT concept of any kind exists in the release

ta_name: ambiguous in TA2 (FIPAT 2nd ed., version 2.07) consulted 2026-11-06 — the record covers lymph nodes AND lymphoid tissue generally; TA2 5191 nodi lymphoidei denotes the nodes only, and lymphoid tissue as such is TA2's chapter grouping (5149 organa lymphoidea), not a term denoting this record.
structure.lymph-nodes.note: The filtering tissue of the system, carried as sourced text; the geometry layer has none of it.
structure.lymph-nodes.nodes: The body carries roughly 500–600 lymph nodes — small, bean-shaped organs that act as filters of the lymph, clustered near the groin, the armpits, the neck, the chest and the abdomen (S2). Within a node, lymph enters by afferent vessels, passes through the subcapsular sinus, the cortex — which holds follicles with germinal centres — and the medulla with its cords and sinuses, and leaves by efferent vessels (S2).
structure.lymph-nodes.tonsils: The tonsils are lymphoid nodules arranged along the inner surface of the pharynx: the pharyngeal tonsil at the roof of the posterior wall of the superior nasopharynx — called the adenoid when swollen — and the palatine tonsils on either side; they carry an incomplete capsule and tonsillar crypts (S2).
structure.lymph-nodes.malt: Beyond the nodes, lymphoid follicles aggregate under mucous membranes as mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) across the gastrointestinal tract, breast, lungs and eyes (S2). In the small intestine these aggregates are Peyer's patches, whose M (microfold) cells sample the gut lumen; the appendix also carries MALT, and bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue (BALT) sits along the bifurcations of the bronchi (S2). The appendix itself is the digestive module's record (Milestone 11); no MALT structure has a concept in the release.

gland.pituitary-gland.name: Pituitary gland
gland.pituitary-gland.note: The release's only intracranial endocrine gland with geometry, and one of only three endocrine glands it carries at all.
gland.pituitary-gland.position: A pea-sized oval gland suspended from the underside of the brain by the infundibulum, seated in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone and roofed by the diaphragma sellae (S1).
gland.pituitary-gland.parts: Two functionally distinct parts. The anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) is glandular epithelium derived from Rathke's pouch, an ectodermal outpouching of the roof of the pharynx; its regions are the pars distalis — the largest and most hormonally active — the pars intermedia and the pars tuberalis (S1). The posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) is neurosecretory tissue derived from the embryonic forebrain and is functionally an extension of the hypothalamus (S1). The release carries the gland as an undivided leaf in both tables: no lobe or part of it exists as a concept (probe-verified), so the parts are sourced text on this record.
gland.pituitary-gland.products: Anterior lobe (S4, Table 17.3): growth hormone (GH), prolactin (PRL), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinising hormone (LH). Intermediate zone: melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH) (S4). Posterior lobe: it synthesises nothing itself — it stores and releases antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and oxytocin, which are synthesised in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus (S1, S4).
gland.pituitary-gland.relations: Anteriorly the sphenoid sinus — the route of trans-sphenoidal surgical access. Superiorly the diaphragma sellae and the optic chiasm: an expanding pituitary adenoma presses on the chiasm and produces bitemporal hemianopia. Laterally the cavernous sinuses. Posteriorly the posterior intercavernous sinus, the dorsum sellae, the basilar artery and the pons; inferiorly the sphenoid sinus again (S1).
gland.pituitary-gland.vasculature: The anterior lobe is fed through the hypophyseal portal system: the superior hypophyseal artery, a branch of the internal carotid, supplies a primary capillary plexus in the median eminence; portal veins carry that blood to a secondary plexus in the anterior lobe, delivering hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones at high concentration (S1). The posterior lobe is supplied by the superior hypophyseal, infundibular and inferior hypophyseal arteries; the gland drains by hypophyseal veins (S1).
gland.pituitary-gland.control: The hypothalamus — the nervous module's record brain.hypothalamus, the floor of the diencephalon anterior and inferior to the thalamus — is both a neural and an endocrine structure (S4): it governs the anterior lobe through the portal blood supply (S1) and owns the posterior lobe's hormones outright, the lobe being its own axonal extension (S1, S4).

gland.thyroid-gland.name: Thyroid gland
verify: no BP3D 4.0 concept exists for this structure (probe-verified over all six release tables by tools/endo_map.py); the record is sourced text only and links no geometry — the release contains no thyroid gland concept in either parts list; every 'thyroid' name it carries is the thyroid cartilage (skeletal module), the inferior thyroid arteries (cardiovascular module) or the sternothyroid and cricothyroid muscles (muscular module)

arterial_supply: the inferior thyroid arteries are cardiovascular inventory records (artery.left-inferior-thyroid-artery, artery.right-inferior-thyroid-artery), resolved by the checker; the superior thyroid artery has no cardiovascular record of its own because its parent, the external carotid artery, is one of the concepts Milestone 5 found absent from the release
gland.thyroid-gland.note: Sourced-text record: the dataset carries the gland's arteries, its cartilage namesake and the muscles named for it, but not the gland.
gland.thyroid-gland.position: In the anterior neck, spanning vertebral levels C5 to T1: two lobes joined across the midline by a central isthmus, the whole gland butterfly-shaped, its lobes wrapping the cricoid cartilage and the superior tracheal rings, enclosed in the pretracheal fascia of the visceral compartment of the neck (S2).
gland.thyroid-gland.structure: The working unit is the thyroid follicle: spheres of follicular cells around a colloid store, and the follicles are the site of hormone production (S5). Between them sit the parafollicular cells (S5). Each lobe carries parathyroid glands embedded in it, primarily on its posterior surface (S5) — see the companion record gland.parathyroid-glands.
gland.thyroid-gland.products: The follicles produce the metabolic hormones thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), for which iodine is an essential component; they raise the basal metabolic rate (S5). The parafollicular cells produce calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium (S5).
gland.thyroid-gland.arterial_supply: The superior thyroid artery, the first branch of the external carotid artery, descends to the upper pole close to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery and approaches the gland close to the recurrent laryngeal nerve. In about 10% of people a thyroid ima artery arises from the brachiocephalic trunk (S2).
gland.thyroid-gland.venous_drainage: A venous plexus on the gland drains by the superior, middle and inferior thyroid veins: the superior and middle veins end in the internal jugular vein, the inferior veins in the brachiocephalic vein (S2).
gland.thyroid-gland.nerves_at_risk: The recurrent laryngeal nerve — a branch of the vagus (the nervous module's clinical record nerve.cn-10-vagus) — is the surgically load-bearing relation of this gland. It branches from the vagus in the chest, hooks around the right subclavian artery on the right and around the arch of the aorta on the left, ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove and passes underneath the thyroid gland to reach the larynx it innervates; it lies close to the inferior thyroid artery and is at risk in thyroid surgery (S2). The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs close to the superior thyroid artery at the upper pole (S2).
gland.thyroid-gland.lymphatic_drainage: Lymph drains to the paratracheal and deep cervical lymph nodes (S2). Neither group exists as a concept in the release — the lymphatic module's census carries no lymph node of any kind — so this drainage is sourced text only.
gland.thyroid-gland.control: Secretion is not under direct nervous control — the sympathetic fibres the gland receives do not govern it (S2); it is pituitary-regulated: thyrotropin-releasing hormone drives thyroid-stimulating hormone, TSH drives T4 and T3 release, and the thyroid hormones feed back negatively on the axis (S2, S5).

gland.parathyroid-glands.name: Parathyroid glands
verify: no BP3D 4.0 concept exists for this structure (probe-verified over all six release tables by tools/endo_map.py); the record is sourced text only and links no geometry — 'parathyroid' scores zero hits in both parts lists and in all six release tables
arterial_supply: no value asserted — none of the sources consulted in this session states the parathyroid glands' arterial supply in citable form; the field stays null rather than unsourced
gland.parathyroid-glands.note: Sourced-text record; the glands' surgical weight is inverse to their size, and the dataset carries no trace of them.
gland.parathyroid-glands.position: Tiny, round glands usually embedded in the posterior surface of the thyroid gland (S6); most people have four, though occasionally more are found in the tissues of the neck or chest (S6). Each is separated from the thyroid tissue by its own thick connective-tissue capsule (S6).
gland.parathyroid-glands.products: Parathyroid hormone (PTH), produced and secreted by the glands' chief cells in response to low blood calcium (S6).
gland.parathyroid-glands.function: PTH defends blood calcium: it stimulates osteoclasts to release calcium from bone, inhibits osteoblasts, increases calcium reabsorption in the kidney tubules, and initiates the production of calcitriol, the active form of vitamin D (S6). Its antagonist is calcitonin, secreted by the thyroid's parafollicular cells (S6) — the pairing that makes the two glands one surgical field.
gland.parathyroid-glands.cells: The chief cells are the primary functional cells of the gland, producing and secreting PTH; the oxyphil cells' function is not clear (S6).
gland.parathyroid-glands.relations: The glands sit within the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes, inside the thyroid's surgical field and separated from its tissue only by their capsule (S6) — which is why they, and the recurrent laryngeal nerve beside them, are what thyroid surgery must not take with the gland (see gland.thyroid-gland, nerves_at_risk).

gland.adrenal-gland.name: Adrenal glands
verify: no BP3D 4.0 concept exists for the adrenal cortex, the adrenal medulla or any cortical zone (probe-verified over all six release tables); the cortex and medulla fields are sourced text on the two whole-gland records
gland.adrenal-gland.note: Owned by this module per the release's own filing (Milestone 12 finding): the glands are direct members of the endocrine system in PART-OF and instances of the adrenal class in IS-A; Milestone 12's urinary census pointed here and this record closes that pointer.
gland.adrenal-gland.position: Paired glands seated over the medial aspect of the upper poles of the kidneys, in the posterior abdomen between the superomedial kidney and the diaphragm; retroperitoneal, with parietal peritoneum on their anterior surface only (S3). The right gland is pyramidal, the left semi-lunar (S3). The perinephric (renal, Gerota) fascia encloses each gland with its kidney and attaches to the diaphragmatic crura, but fibrous tissue separates gland from kidney within it (S3) — the anatomical basis on which the urinary module censused these glands as this module's cross-reference rather than its own.
gland.adrenal-gland.cortex: The outer zone of the gland, derived from embryonic mesoderm, yellowish, secreting the cholesterol-derived corticosteroids and androgens (S3). Its three zones run superficial to deep in a fixed order: the zona glomerulosa secretes the mineralocorticoids (aldosterone); the zona fasciculata secretes the corticosteroids (cortisol) and a small amount of androgens; the zona reticularis secretes the androgens (dehydroepiandrosterone) and a small amount of corticosteroids (S3).
gland.adrenal-gland.medulla: The central zone, dark brown, derived from ectodermal neural crest: its chromaffin cells secrete the catecholamines (adrenaline) and enkephalins, the hormonal arm of the flight-or-fight response (S3).
gland.adrenal-gland.products: Cortex: mineralocorticoids — aldosterone (zona glomerulosa); corticosteroids — cortisol (zona fasciculata); androgens — dehydroepiandrosterone (zona reticularis) (S3). Medulla: catecholamines, principally adrenaline, with enkephalins (S3). Hormone names are asserted here only as the consulted source names them.
gland.adrenal-gland.relations: Right gland: anteriorly the inferior vena cava and the right lobe of the liver, posteriorly the right crus of the diaphragm. Left gland: anteriorly the stomach, the pancreas and the spleen, posteriorly the left crus (S3). Arteries and nerves enter at numerous sites around each gland, while veins and lymphatics leave through a hilum (S3).
gland.adrenal-gland.arterial_supply: Three tiers (S3): the superior adrenal arteries from the inferior phrenic arteries; the middle adrenal arteries directly from the abdominal aorta; the inferior adrenal arteries from the renal arteries. The cardiovascular module carries the middle and inferior tiers under the release's own naming as the middle and inferior suprarenal arteries (records artery.left-middle-suprarenal-artery, artery.right-middle-suprarenal-artery, artery.left-inferior-suprarenal-artery, artery.right-inferior-suprarenal-artery), resolved by the checker.
gland.adrenal-gland.venous_drainage: Asymmetric, and surgically load-bearing for it: the right adrenal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava, the left adrenal vein into the left renal vein (S3). The cardiovascular module carries both as the suprarenal veins (vein.right-suprarenal-vein, vein.left-suprarenal-vein).
gland.adrenal-gland.innervation: From the coeliac plexus and the greater splanchnic nerves (S3); the medulla is driven directly by myelinated preganglionic fibres, mainly from T10 to L1 — the medulla is, in effect, a sympathetic ganglion that secretes into the blood (S3).
gland.adrenal-gland.lymphatics: Lymph drains to the lumbar lymph nodes through two plexuses, one deep to the capsule and one within the medulla (S3). No lumbar node exists as a concept in the release (lymphatic module census).

gland.pineal-gland.name: Pineal gland
verify: geometry held by the nervous module: the release files the pineal body inside the nervous system tree, where it is the nervous inventory record brain.pineal-body (FMA62033, Milestone 9); this record carries the gland's endocrine account and does not duplicate the mesh link
gland.pineal-gland.note: Cross-module record: geometry in the nervous module (brain.pineal-body), function here — the release's filing split, kept, with each side pointing at the other.
gland.pineal-gland.position: A tiny endocrine gland of the diencephalon, lying inferior but somewhat posterior to the thalamus (S7). The release files the pineal body inside the nervous system tree — under the epithalamus — and the nervous module holds its geometry; this record is its endocrine account.
gland.pineal-gland.products: Melatonin, an amine hormone derived from serotonin, produced and secreted by the gland's pinealocytes (S7).
gland.pineal-gland.function: Melatonin secretion entrains the circadian rhythms — sleepiness and wakefulness, and with them appetite and body temperature (S7). The source is explicit that the gland's functions are not entirely understood (S7); nothing further is asserted here.
gland.pineal-gland.regulation: Secretion varies with environmental light: photons striking the retina signal the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus, which relays through the spinal cord to the pineal and inhibits melatonin production — levels fall and wakefulness follows; in darkness production rises and drowsiness follows (S7).

gland.pancreatic-islets.name: Pancreatic islets
verify: no BP3D 4.0 concept exists for this structure (probe-verified over all six release tables by tools/endo_map.py); the record is sourced text only and links no geometry — 'islet' and 'langerhans' score zero hits in both parts lists and in all six release tables
gland.pancreatic-islets.note: Sourced-text record on another module's organ: the endocrine pancreas exists in the clinical layer only, exactly as far as the consulted source describes it.
gland.pancreatic-islets.definition: Clusters of endocrine cells scattered through the pancreas — formerly called the islets of Langerhans — which secrete glucagon, insulin, somatostatin and pancreatic polypeptide into the blood (S8). The pancreas that hosts them is primarily an exocrine gland (S8).
gland.pancreatic-islets.cell_types: Four cell varieties, in the proportions the consulted source gives: alpha cells about 20% of the islet, beta cells about 75%, delta cells about 4%, and PP cells about 1% (S8).
gland.pancreatic-islets.products: Alpha cells secrete glucagon, which raises blood glucose and is released when glucose is low; beta cells secrete insulin, which reduces blood glucose; delta cells secrete somatostatin, which inhibits the release of both glucagon and insulin; PP cells secrete pancreatic polypeptide (S8).
gland.pancreatic-islets.host_organ: The host organ is the pancreas — a long, slender organ lying mostly posterior to the bottom half of the stomach (S8) — which is the digestive module's inventory record pancreas and clinical record organ.pancreas (Milestone 11); the islets are censused there as this module's cross-reference boundary in reverse. No islet, and no part of the endocrine pancreas, has a concept in the release.

pathway.male-reproductive-pathway.name: Male reproductive pathway
verify: the pathway record links no geometry itself: its stations' geometry is held by this module's organ records where the release carries them (testis, epididymis, seminal vesicles, prostate, erectile tissues), and the ductus deferens and ejaculatory duct stations have no BP3D 4.0 concept at all (probe-verified over all six release tables by tools/repro_map.py)
ta_name: not found in TA2 (FIPAT 2nd ed., version 2.07) consulted 2026-11-06 — project pathway construct (the sperm pathway as a route, not a structure); no TA2 term denotes it.
pathway.male-reproductive-pathway.note: The pathway crosses two module boundaries by design: it begins in this module's gonad and ends in the urinary module's urethra, and two of its stations are dataset absences carried as sourced text.
pathway.male-reproductive-pathway.description: The route sperm take from production to exit. Formed in the seminiferous tubules of the testis, sperm leave the testis through the efferent ductules for the epididymis, and at ejaculation are driven along the ductus deferens, through the ejaculatory duct and out through the urethra — after they leave the testes, the sperm passes through the epididymis, ductus deferens, ejaculatory duct, and urethra (S3, S4).
pathway.male-reproductive-pathway.urethra_relationship: The pathway's terminal segment is the urethra — a structure this module does not own. The release carries exactly one urethra concept (FMA19667), unsexed and undivided, and the urinary module (Milestone 12) holds it as its inventory record 'urethra', with clinical record structure.urethra: the urethra is the shared terminal channel of the urinary and male reproductive systems, running from the bladder to the external urethral orifice at the tip of the penis, a passageway for sperm and reproductive fluids and for urine — though never both at once, sphincters contracting to keep urine out of it while reproductive fluids pass (S3). It is censused there and cross-referenced here, never duplicated; its three regions (prostatic, membranous, spongy) exist in this module only as the pathway's sourced text, there being no regional urethra concepts in the release (S3, S4, S10).
pathway.male-reproductive-pathway.glands_in_order: In the order their secretions join the stream: the seminal vesicles first, their duct joining the ductus deferens at its ampulla to form the ejaculatory duct, so their fluid enters with the sperm (S3, S4); the prostate next, its ducts opening into the prostatic urethra as the fluid passes (S2, S3); the bulbourethral glands last into the penile urethra — in fact discharged before the semen itself, as the pre-ejaculate (S3, S4).
pathway.male-reproductive-pathway.semen_composition: Sperm make up only about 5 percent of the final volume of semen; the seminal vesicles contribute approximately 60 percent, the prostate and the bulbourethral glands most of the remainder (S4).
pathway.male-reproductive-pathway.clinical_note: Vasectomy interrupts the pathway at its most accessible station: the ductus deferens is cut and sealed inside the scrotum, where it is bundled in the spermatic cord — clinicians regard the procedure as permanent (S4). The station is one the dataset does not carry at all.

organ.testis.name: Testis
organ.testis.note: The male gonad is the dataset's best-served reproductive organ: geometry, its arteries and veins in the cardiovascular module, and this record — against the female gonad's sourced text over a total dataset absence (organ.ovary).
organ.testis.description: The male gonads: paired ellipsoid organs housed within the scrotum, each suspended by the spermatic cord, the epididymis applied to the posterolateral surface of each, and the left testis usually sitting lower than the right (S1).
organ.testis.parts: Each testis is divided by septa of its dense fibrous capsule, the tunica albuginea, into lobules of seminiferous tubules — OpenStax counts 300 to 400 lobules (S4) — where sperm develop, surrounded by sustentacular (Sertoli) cells, with the interstitial (Leydig) cells between the tubules producing testosterone (S1, S4). Formed sperm pass from the tubules into the straight tubules, then the rete testis, and leave through the efferent ductules (S4). Over the capsule lies the tunica vaginalis, a serous peritoneal sac covering the front and sides (S1, S4). No part, covering or tubule has a concept in the release — the data carries the organs as undivided volumes.
organ.testis.function: Spermatogenesis and androgen production: the testes produce sperm and androgens — principally testosterone, the hormone that supports male reproductive physiology — and are active throughout the reproductive lifespan (S1, S4).
organ.testis.dimension: Each testis is approximately 4 to 5 cm in length (S4). Sperm production proceeds more efficiently at 2 to 4 °C below core body temperature, which the scrotal position provides (S4).
organ.testis.arterial_supply: The paired testicular arteries arise from the abdominal aorta and descend through the inguinal canal in the spermatic cord — the route of the testis' own descent from the posterior abdominal wall; the cremasteric artery (from the inferior epigastric) and the artery of the ductus deferens (from the inferior vesical) anastomose with them (S1). The cardiovascular module carries both as records artery.right-testicular-artery and artery.left-testicular-artery, resolved by the checker (S10).
organ.testis.venous_drainage: The pampiniform plexus drains into the testicular veins, asymmetrically: the left testicular vein ends in the left renal vein, the right directly in the inferior vena cava (S1). Carried by the cardiovascular module as vein.right-testicular-vein and vein.left-testicular-vein (S10).
organ.testis.lymphatic_drainage: To the lumbar (para-aortic) lymph nodes, following the gonadal vessels back to their origin — not to the inguinal nodes, which drain the scrotal skin instead (S1). No lumbar node exists as a concept in the release (lymphatic module census), so this drainage is sourced text only.
organ.testis.innervation: Via the testicular plexus, derived from the renal and aortic plexuses (S1). No testicular nerve concept exists in the release (nervous module census), so this is sourced text only.
organ.testis.relations: Within the scrotum behind the penis, one testis per compartment of the scrotal septum (S4); the epididymis sits posterolateral (S1). Each testis reached the scrotum by descending from the posterior abdominal wall through the inguinal canal during development, carrying its vessels, nerves and lymphatics with it (S1).

structure.epididymis.name: Epididymis
verify: arterial_supply: no value asserted — none of the sources consulted in this session states the epididymis' own arterial supply in citable form (the testicular arteries are recorded on organ.testis); the field stays null rather than unsourced
structure.epididymis.note: The only duct of the male pathway the release carries — the pathway is continuous in the data from the testis to here, and broken from here on.
structure.epididymis.description: A long, tightly coiled tube forming a comma-shaped organ along the superior and posterior margins of the testis — a single heavily coiled duct, not a bundle of ducts (S1, S3).
structure.epididymis.parts: Head, body and tail. The head is formed by the efferent ductules arriving from the rete testis; the body is the coiled duct itself; the tail is where mature sperm are stored and where the ductus deferens begins (S1, S3).
structure.epididymis.function: Maturation and storage: sperm leave the testis immature and incapable of fertilising an ovum, complete their maturation as they move through the epididymis, and are stored, fertile, in its tail until ejaculation (S3, S4).
structure.epididymis.dimension: About 6 metres long if straightened (S3, S4); sperm take an average of about 12 days to transit its coils (S4).
structure.epididymis.relations: Applied to the superior and posterior margins of the testis within the scrotum, continuous at its tail with the ductus deferens (S3).

duct.ductus-deferens.name: Ductus deferens (vas deferens)
verify: no BP3D 4.0 concept exists for this structure (probe-verified over all six release tables by tools/repro_map.py); the record is sourced text only and links no geometry — 'ductus deferens', 'vas deferens', 'spermatic' and 'ejaculat' all score zero hits in both parts lists and in all six release tables; the ejaculatory duct it ends in is likewise absent, so the male pathway's middle is missing from the data entire
duct.ductus-deferens.note: Sourced-text record for the pathway's missing middle: the duct a vasectomy interrupts has no more presence in the dataset than the ovary does.
duct.ductus-deferens.description: A fibromuscular tube continuous with the tail of the epididymis, conducting sperm from the scrotum to the ejaculatory duct (S3, S4).
duct.ductus-deferens.course: It begins at the tail of the epididymis and turns sharply upward along the posterior margin of the testis; bundled in the spermatic cord, it enters the abdominopelvic cavity through the inguinal canal, passes along the lateral pelvic wall, crosses over the ureter and the posterior portion of the urinary bladder, and descends behind the bladder toward the prostate, enlarging into the ampulla just before it reaches the gland (S3, S4).
duct.ductus-deferens.function: Transport and proximal storage: sperm are stored in its proximal portion near the epididymis, and peristaltic contraction propels them through it at ejaculation (S3).
duct.ductus-deferens.parts: Its named dilation is the ampulla, the flask-like enlargement just before the prostate, where it joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct (S3, S4). The spermatic cord that carries its proximal portion also contains the testicular artery and veins, lymphatics, the testicular nerve and the cremaster muscle (S3).
duct.ductus-deferens.clinical_note: Because the duct is physically accessible within the scrotum, surgical sterilisation — vasectomy — cuts and seals a small section of it; the procedure is considered permanent (S4).

gland.seminal-vesicles.name: Seminal vesicles
verify: arterial_supply: no value asserted — none of the sources consulted in this session states the seminal vesicles' arterial supply in citable form; the field stays null rather than unsourced
gland.seminal-vesicles.note: Geometry-linked, unlike the duct they join: the release carries the glands but not the ductus deferens or the ejaculatory duct they complete.
gland.seminal-vesicles.description: Paired glands whose ducts join the ampullae of the ductus deferens behind the bladder to form the ejaculatory ducts, which then pass through the prostate and empty into the urethra (S3, S4).
gland.seminal-vesicles.function: Their secretion contributes approximately 60 percent of semen volume: rich in fructose, which the sperm's mitochondria burn for the ATP of movement, and alkaline, neutralising the acidic environment of the vagina; its prostaglandins act on the cervix (S4). Sperm are immobile until mixed with the seminal glands' secretions (S4).
gland.seminal-vesicles.relations: Posterior to the urinary bladder, the ductus deferens arched over it to meet them (S4); the ejaculatory ducts they form traverse the prostate gland (S3).

gland.prostate.name: Prostate gland
verify: lymphatic_drainage: no value asserted — none of the sources consulted in this session states the prostate's lymphatic drainage in citable form; the field stays null rather than unsourced
gland.prostate.note: The release's only genital-system member gets the tranche's fullest gland record — geometry, zones, relations and the nerve-sparing relation included.
gland.prostate.description: The largest accessory gland of the male reproductive system: a walnut-sized gland of muscular and glandular tissue — about two-thirds glandular, one-third fibromuscular — surrounding the prostatic urethra at the base of the urinary bladder (S2, S4). It is the one member the release files under its own genital system.
gland.prostate.parts: McNeal's zones (S2): the central zone, about 25 percent, surrounds the ejaculatory ducts; the transitional zone, 5–10 percent, surrounds the urethra and is where benign prostatic hyperplasia arises; the peripheral zone, about 65 percent, is the posterior main body — the zone palpable on rectal examination; and the anterior fibromuscular stroma is the fourth zone. The traditional lobes are also described by the source (S2). The release carries the gland as one undivided concept: no zone or lobe exists in the data.
gland.prostate.function: It excretes a milky fluid into the passing semen: proteolytic enzymes via prostatic ducts opening into the prostatic urethra — among them prostate-specific antigen (PSA), which liquefies semen after its initial coagulation — with citric acid and the antibiotic seminalplasmin (S2, S4).
gland.prostate.relations: Inferior to the neck of the bladder, superior to the external urethral sphincter, levator ani inferolaterally, and the ampulla of the rectum posteriorly — the relation by which the peripheral zone is palpated on digital rectal examination (S2). Its thin fibrous capsule is adventitia-like, not a true capsule (S2).
gland.prostate.arterial_supply: Prostatic arteries arising mainly from the internal iliac artery, with contributions from the internal pudendal and middle rectal arteries (S2).
gland.prostate.venous_drainage: The prostatic venous plexus drains into the internal iliac veins, and communicates with the internal vertebral venous plexus (Batson's) (S2).
gland.prostate.innervation: From the inferior hypogastric plexus (S2). The neurovascular bundles flank the gland on their way to the corpora cavernosa — the anatomical basis of nerve-sparing prostatectomy (S2).

gland.bulbourethral-glands.name: Bulbourethral glands (Cowper's glands)
verify: no BP3D 4.0 concept exists for this structure (probe-verified over all six release tables by tools/repro_map.py); the record is sourced text only and links no geometry — 'bulbourethral' and 'cowper' score zero hits in both parts lists and in all six release tables

position: no value asserted — none of the sources consulted in this session places the glands (the deep perineal pouch) in citable form, and the pouch itself has no concept in the release; the field stays null rather than unsourced
gland.bulbourethral-glands.note: The third accessory gland completes the pathway's gland order as sourced text; the release carries its two companions but not it.
gland.bulbourethral-glands.description: Two small glands whose ducts open into the penile (spongy) urethra (S3, S4).
gland.bulbourethral-glands.function: They release a thick, salty mucus that lubricates the end of the urethra and the vagina and cleans urine residues from the penile urethra; the fluid is released after arousal and shortly before the semen — the pre-ejaculate — and can pick up sperm already present in the urethra (S4).

organ.penis.name: Penis
verify: innervation: no value asserted — none of the sources consulted in this session states the penile innervation in citable form; the pudendal nerve is not asserted here, and no penile nerve concept exists in the release (nervous module census)
organ.penis.note: An organ the dataset represents only in pieces: three erectile structures here, five vessels in the cardiovascular module, and no whole-organ concept anywhere.
organ.penis.description: The male organ of copulation, delivering sperm into the female reproductive tract: flaccid for non-sexual actions such as urination, turgid and rod-like with sexual arousal (S4). The release has no penis concept — no concept is named 'penis' (exact-name probe-verified) — so this record is assembled from the three erectile structures the release does carry, with its vessels in the cardiovascular module (S10).
organ.penis.parts: The shaft is composed of three column-like chambers of erectile tissue: the two larger lateral corpora cavernosa, which together make up the bulk of the penis, and the smaller corpus spongiosum, felt as a raised ridge on the erect penis, which surrounds the spongy (penile) urethra (S4). The end of the penis is the glans penis, its skin rich in nerve endings; the skin of the shaft extends over the glans as a collar, the prepuce (foreskin) (S4). The prepuce has no concept in the release — 'prepuce' scores zero hits — and is text here only.
organ.penis.function: Copulation and semen delivery, and — through the spongy urethra it encloses — the exit of urine (S4). Erection is vasocongestion: on arousal, nitric oxide from nerve endings relaxes the smooth muscle of the penile arteries, the erectile chambers fill faster than the veins drain them, and the pressure of the filled chambers compresses the thin-walled venules, trapping the blood (S4).
organ.penis.arterial_supply: The penile arteries whose dilation drives erection (S4) are carried by name in the release only in the cardiovascular module: the dorsal arteries of the penis, records artery.right-dorsal-artery-of-penis and artery.left-dorsal-artery-of-penis (S10).
organ.penis.venous_drainage: The veins the release names for this organ are the cardiovascular module's records vein.deep-dorsal-vein-of-penis, vein.right-superficial-dorsal-vein-of-penis and vein.left-superficial-dorsal-vein-of-penis (S10); the erectile mechanism compresses the penile venules against drainage (S4).

pathway.female-reproductive-pathway.name: Female reproductive pathway
verify: no BP3D 4.0 concept exists for this structure (probe-verified over all six release tables by tools/repro_map.py); the record is sourced text only and links no geometry — for every station of the pathway, not one structure: 'ovary', 'uterus', 'vagina' and 'uterine' all score zero hits in both parts lists and in all six release tables
ta_name: not found in TA2 (FIPAT 2nd ed., version 2.07) consulted 2026-11-06 — project pathway construct (a route, not a structure); no TA2 term denotes it.
pathway.female-reproductive-pathway.note: A pathway with no geometry at any station — the exact inverse of the male pathway, whose first stations are the dataset's best-served organs.
pathway.female-reproductive-pathway.description: The route of the oocyte, and in pregnancy of the conceptus: the ovary produces and releases the oocyte, the uterine tube conveys it to the uterus, the uterus receives it — the usual site of implantation — and the vagina is the tract's canal to the exterior (S5, S6, S9).
pathway.female-reproductive-pathway.function: Gamete production in the ovary, transport along the tube, implantation and gestation in the uterus, and delivery through the vagina: the internal organs work together as a conduit for sperm to reach the egg and for the development and birth of the fetus (S9).
pathway.female-reproductive-pathway.dataset_note: Every station of this pathway is a dataset absence: not one of these structures has a concept in BP3D 4.0 (probe-verified per sex line by tools/repro_map.py). The pathway record exists so that the module states the female tract's sourced anatomy and its total absence in one place; the only female geometry in the module is the mons pubis, which is not a station of this pathway but the surface landmark at its end (structure.mons-pubis).

organ.ovary.name: Ovary
verify: no BP3D 4.0 concept exists for this structure (probe-verified over all six release tables by tools/repro_map.py); the record is sourced text only and links no geometry — the absence is recorded on this record itself, as the milestone directs: 'ovary', 'ovarian', 'ovarian follicle' and 'corpus luteum' score zero hits in both parts lists and in all six release tables; Milestone 13 recorded the same absence at the endocrine boundary and this record inherits it
organ.ovary.note: The module's headline record: a fully sourced account (tier A on fields) of the female gonad over a total dataset absence — the mirror image of organ.testis, which has geometry, vessels and a census line.
organ.ovary.description: The female gonads: paired, oval organs attached to the posterior surface of the broad ligament of the uterus by the mesovarium, a fold of peritoneum continuous with the ovaries' outer surface, with neurovascular structures entering at the hilum (S5).
organ.ovary.parts: Three histological components (S5): the surface, a simple cuboidal epithelium (the germinal epithelium) over a dense connective-tissue capsule; the cortex, a connective-tissue stroma carrying numerous ovarian follicles, each an oocyte surrounded by follicular cells; and the medulla, loose connective tissue with a rich neurovascular network entering at the hilum. No component has a concept in the release.
organ.ovary.function: To produce oocytes (female gametes) in preparation for fertilisation, and to produce the sex steroid hormones oestrogen and progesterone in response to the pituitary gonadotrophins LH and FSH (S5).
organ.ovary.dimension: Paired ovals some 2 to 3 cm long, seated in the pelvic cavity: the gonads develop in the mesonephric ridge and descend through the abdomen, but unlike the testes the ovaries stop in the pelvis (S5, S7).
organ.ovary.ligaments: Two peritoneal ligaments (S5): the suspensory ligament of the ovary, extending from the mesovarium to the pelvic wall and containing the neurovascular structures; and the ligament of the ovary, extending from the ovary to the fundus of the uterus, then continuing from the uterus to the labium majus as the round ligament of the uterus.
organ.ovary.arterial_supply: The paired ovarian arteries arise directly from the abdominal aorta, inferior to the renal arteries; there is also a contribution from the uterine arteries (S5). Dataset gap, recorded: the cardiovascular module carries no ovarian artery record, the release having no ovarian vessel concept either (S10) — unlike the testis, whose arteries the sister module holds, this supply has no cross-module pointer to resolve.
organ.ovary.venous_drainage: Paired ovarian veins: the left drains into the left renal vein, the right directly into the inferior vena cava (S5) — the same asymmetry as the testicular veins, and likewise without a cardiovascular record in the release (S10).
organ.ovary.lymphatic_drainage: Lymph from the ovaries drains into the para-aortic nodes (S5). No para-aortic node exists as a concept in the release (lymphatic module census).
organ.ovary.innervation: Sympathetic and parasympathetic fibres from the ovarian and uterine (pelvic) plexuses respectively, reaching the ovary via the suspensory ligament to enter at the hilum (S5).

duct.uterine-tube.name: Uterine tube (Fallopian tube)
verify: no BP3D 4.0 concept exists for this structure (probe-verified over all six release tables by tools/repro_map.py); the record is sourced text only and links no geometry — 'uterine', 'fallopian' and 'fimbria' score zero hits in both parts lists and in all six release tables

regional_subdivisions: the tube's named regions beyond the fimbriae are not asserted — they are not named in citable form in the sources consulted in this session, and no regional concept exists in the release; the field stays null rather than unsourced
duct.uterine-tube.note: Sourced-text record; the fimbriae are its one sourced part, the rest of the tube's regional anatomy flagged rather than filled.
duct.uterine-tube.description: Paired tubes extending laterally from the upper uterus toward the ovaries, serving as the pathway for oocytes from the ovary to the uterine cavity (S7, S9).
duct.uterine-tube.parts: The distal end, nearest the ovary, carries finger-like projections — the fimbriae — which overhang the ovary and receive the released oocyte (S7).
duct.uterine-tube.function: Transport: the tube conveys the oocyte, and after fertilisation the embryo, slowly to the uterus, where implantation follows (S7, S9).

organ.uterus.name: Uterus
verify: no BP3D 4.0 concept exists for this structure (probe-verified over all six release tables by tools/repro_map.py); the record is sourced text only and links no geometry — 'uterus' and 'uterine' score zero hits in both parts lists and in all six release tables, and the wall layers with them: 'endometrium', 'myometrium' and 'perimetrium' are likewise zero-hit probes
organ.uterus.note: Fully sourced (tier A on fields) over a total dataset absence, like organ.ovary: the release contains the ureter this organ's artery crosses, but not the organ.
organ.uterus.description: A thick-walled muscular organ of the female reproductive tract, capable of expansion to accommodate a growing fetus, connected distally to the vagina and laterally to the uterine tubes (S6). It is a secondary sex organ — a component of the tract that matures during puberty under the influence of the ovaries' sex hormones (S6).
organ.uterus.parts: Three parts (S6): the fundus, the top of the uterus above the entry point of the uterine tubes; the body, the usual site for implantation of the blastocyst; and the cervix, the lower part linking the uterus with the vagina, structurally and functionally different to the rest of the uterus.
organ.uterus.function: The maintenance and transportation of gametes (S6), the housing of the implanted conceptus through gestation, and — by the contractions of its myometrium — delivery (S6, S9).
organ.uterus.wall_layers: The fundus and body are composed of three tissue layers (S6): the perimetrium, a double-layered peritoneal membrane; the myometrium, a thick smooth-muscle layer whose cells undergo hypertrophy and hyperplasia during pregnancy; and the endometrium, the inner mucous membrane, whose deep stratum basalis changes little through the cycle and is not shed, while its superficial stratum functionalis proliferates under oestrogen, becomes secretory under progesterone, and is shed at menstruation. No layer has a concept in the release.
organ.uterus.dimension: About 5 cm wide and 7 cm long in the non-pregnant adult (S7).
organ.uterus.position: In the normal adult the uterus is anteverted with respect to the vagina and anteflexed with respect to the cervix, lying immediately posterosuperior to the bladder and anterior to the rectum; its exact location varies with the distension of the bladder (S6).
organ.uterus.ligaments: The tone of the pelvic floor is the primary support; the ligaments secure it further (S6): the broad ligament, a double layer of peritoneum attaching the sides of the uterus to the pelvis and acting as its mesentery; the round ligament, a gubernacular remnant running from the uterine horns to the labia majora via the inguinal canal, maintaining anteversion; the ovarian ligament, joining the ovaries to the uterus; the cardinal ligament at the base of the broad ligament, from the cervix to the lateral pelvic walls, containing the uterine artery and vein; and the uterosacral ligament, from the cervix to the sacrum. No ligament has a concept in the release.
organ.uterus.arterial_supply: The uterine artery, a branch of the internal iliac artery (S6). It crosses the ureter approximately 1 cm lateral to the internal os — 'water under the bridge' — the relation that hysterectomy must respect (S6).
organ.uterus.venous_drainage: Via a plexus in the broad ligament that drains into the uterine veins (S6).
organ.uterus.lymphatic_drainage: Via the iliac, sacral, aortic and inguinal lymph nodes (S6). None exists as a concept in the release (lymphatic module census).
organ.uterus.innervation: Sympathetic fibres from the uterovaginal plexus — largely the anterior and intermediate parts of the inferior hypogastric plexus; parasympathetic fibres from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4); the cervix largely by the inferior fibres of the uterovaginal plexus; afferents ascending through the inferior hypogastric plexus to T10–T12 and L1 (S6).

organ.vagina.description: A muscular, epithelium-lined tube known as the vagina connects the vulva to the cervix of the uterus (S9); it is continuous superiorly with the cervix and communicates with the exterior at the vaginal orifice in the vestibule (S7).
organ.vagina.parts: Its upper end meets the cervix in the recess called the fornix (S7). The canal is a muscular tube lined with stratified squamous epithelium over smooth muscle (S7). organ.vagina.function: The tract's canal to the exterior: the internal organs work together as a conduit for sperm to reach the egg during intercourse and for the development and birth of the fetus, and the vagina is that conduit's lower passage, from the cervix to the vestibule (S9).
organ.vagina.dimension: Approximately 10 cm long in the adult (S7).

structure.vulva.description: The external female reproductive organs, known collectively as the vulva: several folds of skin surrounding the urinary and reproductive orifices (S9).
